Petroleum and cargo shipping head the Combined Chiefs' record of February 8, 1945. The chiefs first approved the minutes of their 186th meeting. Then they took up levels of supply of oil products in all theaters. An overall review of cargo shipping followed, built on a joint staff paper.

Admiral Leahy said the American chiefs found the shipping paper acceptable with one change. A date in it should move from April 30 to April 1. Lord Leathers, Britain's transport minister, answered that the change suited him well, if the staffs could match it. The record is dry, but the stakes were real: shipping set the speed of every plan the alliance made.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d486: An air pact with Ireland caused a flap in this short cable from Stettinius to Grew, sent February 7, 1945. The British were disturbed that the United States had made an aviation pact with Ireland without consulting or informing them. Stettinius asked Grew to send a fitting explanation promptly, for the delegation to present to the British. The pact, covering air transport service, had been signed at Washington on February 3, while the conference party was at Malta. Even a side quarrel over air routes reached the Secretary mid-summit.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d86:
At the White House on 8 January 1945, the voting formula came back to the President's desk. Leo Pasvolsky's record of the meeting is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Stettinius, Dunn, Pasvolsky, and Bohlen sat with Roosevelt to plan the coming talks with Churchill and Stalin.

Stettinius warned that without agreement on voting, the United Nations conference might be delayed for a long time. Interest would slacken and opposition could grow. The President said he was determined to press for a decision. Yet he remained puzzled over one case: a dispute between the United States and, say, Mexico, reaching the Council with the United States denied a vote.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d186:
The American chargé in Prague forwarded a Czechoslovak request in a despatch dated July 5, 1945. The short covering letter is document 186 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It transmits the Czechoslovak Foreign Office's note asking that its application be heard by the Big Three.

President Beneš and his government want their request for the transfer of minorities placed on the agenda of the meeting of Truman, Churchill, and Stalin. The minorities in question were chiefly the Sudeten Germans, whose expulsion from Czechoslovakia Prague sought to have the great powers approve. The full note is printed later in the volume. Klieforth's brief letter shows a small state lobbying to get its case onto a table where it had no seat.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d286:
A background paper described Communist gains in Bulgaria, dated July 5, 1945. The paper is document 286 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is one of the country studies made for the President's briefing book.

Since the Fatherland Front took power, the summary says, the Bulgarian Workers' Party, the Communists, has worked hard to tighten its grip. By maneuver and by threats from the party-run militia, moderates have been pushed out of the Agrarian, Social Democratic, and Zveno parties. The Front now faces the vote set for August 26 with a wholly Communist face. The control body still lacks real U.S. and British voice, no U.S. newsmen have been let in, and Soviet troops in the country are said to number 200,000.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d386:
German ships and the Soviet share of them fill an undated memorandum by George Elsey. On May 23, 1945, Stalin had cabled Truman and Churchill a complaint: not one German naval or merchant vessel had surrendered to Soviet forces. How, he asked, would the Soviet Union obtain the one-third of German ships that rightfully and justly should fall to it?

Stalin also wanted the Red Navy to examine all papers on the surrender and state of the German ships. Churchill replied on May 27 that the matters belonged in the general discussion among the three leaders. Elsey's memo assembles the exchange, including Hopkins's report of his own talk with Stalin, for Truman's use.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d486:
The Polish Commission's agreed statement is cabled by Harriman from Moscow on June 23, 1945. The Commission that night agreed a communiqué, for release twenty-four hours later, on the formation of a Provisional Polish Government of National Unity. Harriman sends the text in full for the Department's record.

The communiqué recalls the Commission's mandate. Molotov spoke for the Soviet Union. The British ambassador, Sir Archibald Kerr, spoke for Britain. Harriman himself spoke for the United States. The three were empowered by the Crimea conference to consult with members of the Provisional Government. They were also to consult with other democratic leaders, from Poland itself and from abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d586:
Ambassador Sato reported from Moscow on July 13, 1945, how he delivered the Emperor's message. His cable, in translation, is document 586 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Molotov, it turns out, could not see him that day.

Sato met deputy minister Lozovsky at 5 p.m. instead. He handed over the Emperor's wishes in Russian, addressed to Molotov, with a private note of his own. The note sought Soviet leave for Prince Konoye's visit and help with a plane if leave was granted. Sato stressed that this mission differed from past ones, since it came from the Emperor himself. He asked for an answer in principle before Molotov left for Berlin. Lozovsky doubted an answer could come that fast, as one Soviet party left that very night.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d686:
A second round of Soviet-Turkish talks in Moscow is reported by Ambassador Wilson on June 22, 1945. His secret wire from Ankara is document 686 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Turkish ambassador had seen Molotov again on June 18.

Under instructions, the ambassador told Molotov Turkey could not accept his three points as a basis for discussion. The long talk stayed civil in tone. Molotov then floated a treaty of collaboration and alliance between the two states. He also raised a new point of his own. Moscow might wish to present to Turkey the views of the Balkan states on questions touching them. Turkey's acting foreign minister noted that no such questions were pending. The Balkan states were beaten belligerents under Allied control commissions, and Turkey would not receive claims voiced for them by Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d86:
Ambassador Harriman updated Admiral Leahy from Moscow on June 22, 1945, in a telegram printed as document 86 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. He had asked Foreign Minister Molotov the night before to get Stalin's reaction to the American Chiefs of Staff coming to Berlin with the President.

Molotov said he would consult Stalin at once, but felt quite sure there would be no objection. Harriman also passes on Vyshinsky's urgent request for the size and shape of the President's party, so the Soviets can plan housing. He asks Leahy for a first estimate: chiefs, officers, political advisers, and clerks. The message captures both sides still counting beds and chairs a month before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1086:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh cabled Washington from Athens on August 1, 1945, about Greece's handling of the Yugoslav protest. He had passed the American reply to the prime minister, who made no comment yet. From the British chargé, he gathers that Athens wants the Macedonian question kept quiet. Greek officials suspect the Yugoslav note grew from inexperience, not menace.

Athens would rather settle with Belgrade directly once a new Yugoslav minister arrives. It will study border incidents, but insists no foreign government may intervene over Greek nationals. MacVeagh adds British findings that shrink the charges: refugee numbers near 5,000, and only three of six alleged incident sites can even be identified.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1186:
Clement Attlee wrote to President Truman on 31 July 1945, five days after becoming prime minister. He was already bargaining at the sharp end of the summit. His message carried the voice of the new Labour government in London.

The change of leaders mid-summit could have wrecked the talks. It did not, in part because notes like this one kept the personal channel warm. Attlee's plain style differed from Churchill's grand manner, and the record shows the shift. This message is the new prime minister at work, two days before the conference closed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1286:
On 21 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The chiefs' run of notes by now covered the summit's first full week.

Each note added the services' judgment on the questions of its day. The file they built gave the American team a military brief that grew with the talks. This memorandum is a mid-series piece. Its worth is in the sequence: read in order, the run shows the staff mind at work across the whole conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1386:
Mikołajczyk, Poland's deputy prime minister, wrote a second memorandum on 25 July 1945, the day after his first in this run. The volume prints his papers as a group near its end. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A run of papers by one man lets readers follow a single mind at work under pressure. Mikołajczyk wrote while the Potsdam leaders fixed Poland's western border and argued over its elections. His memoranda were bids to be heard by the powers deciding his country's future without him in the room. Read in sequence, they show hope narrowing day by day, in step with the summit's own calendar.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-86:
Staff of the United States delegation at Potsdam drew up this memorandum on July 24, 1945. Delegation memoranda were the team's daily work tools. They briefed leaders, summed up talks, and set out facts for the next round. This one was kept with the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Because such papers were written for use, not for the public, they tend to be plain and direct. They show the American team thinking on paper between sessions. Read with the formal minutes, they fill in the staff work behind the heads of government. The memo is one piece of a large, careful paper trail.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d786:
Winant answered Mosely on July 27, 1945, in document 786. The ambassador in London replied the same day he was written to. Their exchange sits in the second Potsdam volume as a neat pair. It shows the London end of the Germany planning web during the conference's last week.

Same-day replies mark an urgent, trusted channel. Winant valued Mosely's counsel on the Commission's work. Readers see two veterans closing a question between them. The document adds a human note to the volume's machinery: old colleagues, writing plainly, at the end of a long shared task. Their letters outlast the summit as a record of how it was staffed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d886:
Soviet delegates proposed this addition to the Political Principles for Germany on July 30, 1945. It would help set up a central German administration under the Control Council. Department heads would run foreign trade, industry, finance, transport, and communications.

The bracketed part of the text goes further. It would have the new administration coordinate the provincial governments. Its task would be to see that Control Council decisions are carried out across Germany. The bracketed passage also covers problems of an all-German character. A margin note on the paper records that Secretary Byrnes suggested cutting that bracketed passage.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d986:
Edwin Pauley and William Clayton cabled the Acting Secretary of State from Babelsberg on July 21, 1945. They advise sending Washington's telegram on Rumanian oil shares to Moscow as well, and to Bucharest. Details of Soviet talks over German property in Stockholm should also go to Moscow, in case the Soviets question the embassy's recent note.

The pair report what the American delegation is putting before the conference. A declaration by the United States, Britain, and the USSR, with France if possible, would place German external assets under the occupying powers and the Control Council. Their envoys would act as agents for both. Staff are also drafting a vesting decree for the Control Council.
frus-1964-68v01-d286: A 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note on the August 4 retaliation in Vietnam. The airstrikes. This note provides that context. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
gao-gaoreports-b-297686: CRAssociates took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297986: Knowledge Connections took its May 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298086: Bristol Group doubled its May 2006 protest — two case numbers, one Union Station venture — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299086: Synectic Solutions took its February 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-486: FDIC information security needed sustained progress in 2005, and GAO's report says the agency had to keep up its efforts. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the deposit data deserved protection. The progress had to be sustained. The deposit data deserved protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-686: Exon-Florio's implementation needed strengthening in 2005, and GAO's report says enhancements could improve the law's effectiveness. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the foreign-deal reviews deserved teeth. The implementation had to be stronger. The foreign-deal reviews deserved teeth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-886: Apprenticeship programs needed better data targeting in 2005, and GAO's report says Labor could better use data for oversight. The findings demand the analytics. The report warns that the trainees deserved watched programs. The data had to be used. The trainees deserved watched programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-986: Corporate tech chiefs' roles got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines responsibilities and governance at leading companies. The findings take the measure. The report shows the private-sector CIOs were studied. The roles had to be understood. The private-sector CIOs were studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-386: The bank secrecy framework needed strengthening in 2006, and GAO's report says opportunities existed for FinCEN and regulators to improve it. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the money-laundering net needed tighter mesh. The framework had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-86: The SEC's people management was improving in 2006, and GAO's report says some progress had been made on human capital strategy. The findings give the partial credit. The report warns that the market watchdog's workforce needed tending. The progress had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1186: The full 2007 Government Accountability Office report on U.S. programs helping other countries build disease-surveillance capacity — companion to GAO's testimony on the same subject. It details how American agencies funded labs, training, and reporting systems abroad to catch outbreaks early. The report evaluates whether those investments were creating a genuinely stronger global warning network.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-486: American aid was saving mothers and babies abroad in 2007 — GAO's report says the programs reached far and wide, but the spending details stayed fuzzy. The findings praise the reach and prod the books. The report's standard is fair: good deeds deserve good accounting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-786: The Congressional Award's books got an audit in 2007 — GAO's report grades the youth foundation's finances for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal audit opinion in full. The report shows the watchdog's reach: even Congress's own charities get the once-over.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-86: Surgery-center payments needed a fairer formula in 2007, and GAO's report says Medicare should tie them to the hospital outpatient system. The findings make the case. The report warns that the same procedure should not cost double by address. The price had to be consistent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-986: The drug-benefit rollout's money got a clean-ish bill from GAO in 2007 — spending rules were in place for the new Medicare drug program, though some lapses showed. The findings credit the Social Security Administration's bookkeeping while flagging the cracks. Big new benefit, mostly steady hands on the purse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-486: The Government Accountability Office dug into employment and Training Program Grants: Evaluating Impact and Enhancing Monitoring Would Improve Accountability in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib2-1586:
Gesner's second volume of the Historiae animalium treats the oviparous quadrupeds, the egg-laying four-footed beasts. It first appeared in 1554, and this text is the second edition of 1586. Tortoises, lizards, frogs, and crocodiles fill a class that modern science has long since rearranged.

Gesner works through each creature with names, pictures, habits, and reports from old authors. His patience looks endless, and his woodcuts carry much of the charm. The volume marches steadily on with the same plan as the first. Readers watch the Renaissance survey the created world beast by beast. Few books of its age match its order and scope.
goad-astro-meteorologica-1686:
John Goad was a London schoolmaster and astrologer whose Astro-Meteorologica appeared in 1686. The book matches thirty years of weather observations against the positions of the planets. Goad kept daily records of wind, rain, frost, and storm for the whole span.

He argues that aspects between planets, and their places in the signs, foretell heat, cold, and tempest in usable patterns. His tables let the reader test the claim year by year against his logged weather. The work is a serious early try at weather forecasting by rule, whatever a modern reader makes of its stars.
gospel-james-walker-1886: The Gospel of James, also called the Protevangelium, an early Christian apocryphal infancy gospel. It tells of Mary's birth and Jesus' childhood. This edition preserves that ancient narrative. The historical record keeps it. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
gould-mythical-monsters-1886:
Charles Gould asked a plain question in 1886: what real beasts stand behind the monster tales? Mythical Monsters surveys dragons, sea serpents, and other famed creatures of lore. Gould was a geologist who had worked in China and read its dragon lore at first hand.

He weighs old reports with a cool head and finds big real animals behind many of them. The dragon, the kraken, and the serpent each get a fair hearing and a strict test. His book treats old tales as clues for science, not jokes. It founded a line of study now called cryptozoology.
granada-sinners-guide-1886:
Luis de Granada was a Spanish Dominican whose Sinner's Guide, first published in 1555, guided Catholic devotion for centuries. McKenna's 1886 English translation carries the ascetical masterpiece to a new audience. Granada wrote for ordinary Christians, not only for monks and nuns.

The guide weighs the reasons for a good life, then gives rules for prayer, fasting, speech, and the care of the poor. Its tone is warm and urgent rather than severe, pressing readers toward virtue as gain, not loss. The book is said to have converted millions, and it still anchors Spanish Catholic devotion. Its counsel assumes a reader who wants heaven and fears the cost.
gurney-myers-podmore-phantasms-vol1-1886:
Edmund Gurney, Frederic Myers, and Frank Podmore published Volume 1 of Phantasms of the Living in 1886 for the Society for Psychical Research. They gathered reports of people who seemed to appear to friends or kin at a moment of crisis or death. Their name for such cases was crisis apparitions.

Hundreds of cases fill the volume, drawn from letters and sworn statements, with names, dates, and checks where the authors could make them. The writers argued that chance alone could not explain so many close matches. Their claim, called telepathy, held that one mind could affect another at a distance, and the cases were their proof.
gurney-myers-podmore-phantasms-vol2-1886:
Volume 2 of Phantasms of the Living, published in 1886 by Edmund Gurney, Frederic Myers, and Frank Podmore, completed their large study of crisis apparitions. The first volume had laid out hundreds of cases. Here the authors pressed further into the theory behind them.

More cases appear, sorted by type, along with long discussion of dreams, waking visions, and shared sights. The authors tried to answer critics who blamed lies, poor memory, or chance. They defended telepathy as the best account of their facts. By that they meant a dying or endangered person could impress his image on a distant mind.
gurney-phantasms-of-the-living-1886:
Three keen men counted ghosts with care in Phantasms of the Living, the vast study of 1886. Edmund Gurney, Frederic Myers, and Frank Podmore were chiefs of a new band for the study of such things. Folk oft claim to see a far kin at the hour of that kin's death. The three sought such tales, checked them, and weighed the odds.

Scores of cases fill two fat tomes, each sifted for fraud and flaw. Their claim is that thought can leap from mind to mind. The work founds a whole field of study. Its care still stuns.
hardy-mayor-casterbridge-1886:
Thomas Hardy published The Mayor of Casterbridge in 1886, a novel that opens with a shocking act. Michael Henchard, a drunken hay worker, sells his wife and child at a fair. Sober, he swears off drink for twenty-one years. He rises by hard work to become mayor of Casterbridge.

Henchard's past returns when his wife reappears in town. His pride, temper, and rivalry with a young Scots manager undo him step by step. Hardy builds the fall with the force of Greek tragedy. The town and its corn trade are drawn in rich detail. Many readers rank the novel as Hardy's supreme tragedy of character.
hunter-animal-oeconomy-1786:
Observations on Certain Parts of the Animal Oeconomy gathers John Hunter's comparative anatomy papers of 1786. Animal oeconomy was the era's term for how living bodies run themselves. Hunter compares organs and functions across species to find shared plans. Digestion and the lymphatic system both receive his sharp attention.

One paper treats the electric organs of the torpedo, a fish that stuns its prey. Such studies built the research program behind his fame in surgery. The first edition joins papers that journals had scattered. Readers see Hunter the naturalist behind Hunter the surgeon. His curiosity ranged over all life. The volume explains his standing among scientists.
hunter-venereal-disease-1786:
John Hunter treated venereal disease in a full treatise in 1786, the first study of its kind. He examined syphilis and gonorrhoea with clinical and experimental methods. Cases from his London practice fill the pages with close detail. Hunter sought the laws by which these diseases spread and changed.

The book includes his famous self inoculation trial, which misled him badly. Working before germ theory, he took the two diseases for one poison. That error, and the careful work around it, both shaped later research. The first edition preserves his reasoning in full. Readers see a great surgeon reasoning at the edge of his era's knowledge. History of medicine courses still assign it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luncz-abraham-m:
Abraham Moses Luncz, a Russian scholar who made Jerusalem his life's work, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Kovno on December 9, 1854, he moved to Jerusalem while still very young. Blind for many years, he helped found an institution for the blind there with Dr. Koisewski. He was still living in Jerusalem in 1904.

The article praises his service to the study of the Holy Land. He wrote guidebooks, Palestine annuals, and a Jerusalem almanac covering history, geography, and the land itself. His six-volume Jerusalem yearbook appeared in Hebrew and German between 1881 and 1903. He also ran a Hebrew printing press and began a Palestinian library. A new edition of the Jerusalem Talmud, with his commentary, was in press. The entry honors a blind scholar who mapped his city for others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahanaim-10286:
Mahanaim, a city east of the Jordan, is located and traced in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It first appears where Jacob, returning from Aram, saw a vision of angels. That implies the place was a sanctuary from a very early period. In Joshua's allotments it belonged to Gad and was assigned as a Levitical city. It stood near the river Jabbok.

The article follows the city's brief hour in Israel's history. Abner brought Saul's son Ish-bosheth there and made it his capital. David later fled to Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion and stayed until recalled. Solomon placed one of his supply officers there. After Shishak's invasion the city vanishes from the record, perhaps destroyed in resisting him. Its name seems dual in form, read as two camps. Scholars still argue over its exact site, most placing it near the wadi Ajlun.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mar-10386:
Mar, an Aramaic word for lord, is traced through Jewish usage in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. Daniel addresses the king as Mari, my lord, in the Bible. In Palestinian schools Mari and Rabbi were the polite address for sages. King Jehoshaphat, the Talmud says, rose to greet a scholar with both titles.

The article shows how address became a fixed title in Babylonia. There Mar stood before a scholar's name, as with Mar Samuel and Mar Ukba. Abaye called his uncle and teacher simply Mar, with no name added. A scholar's son citing his father said Abba Mari, my father, my lord. In the geonic period Mar and Rab combined into the double title Mar Rab. The prayer Yekum Purkan still calls scholars our lords and masters. The entry follows one small word from courtesy into the official style of the Babylonian academies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-moses-g:
Moses Gerson Michael, born on August 15, 1862, at Jefferson, Georgia, was an American merchant who built a dry-goods fortune at Athens. Cyrus Adler and Herbert E. Choate wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He graduated from the University of Georgia with highest honors and went straight into business with his brother Simon.

Michael's money and energy fed the growth of northeastern Georgia, where he backed several large industrial ventures. He held the rank of lieutenant-colonel in the state militia and served as aide-de-camp to Governor Candler, with a seat on the Democratic committee of his congressional district. At home in Athens he ran the Jewish Sabbath-school for years as his own special charge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-dato-b:
Mordecai Dato — Dato being the Italian of Nathan — was a Ferrara poet of the sixteenth century, recorded by Wilhelm Bacher and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He annotated Samuel Gallico's cabalistic 'Asis Rimmonim with notes he called Hagahot, glosses, when it was printed at Venice in 1601.

Azariah dei Rossi credits him with a book on the coming of the Messiah, Migdal Dawid. His lasting work was verse: many liturgical poems survive in manuscript, and one, for the eve of the Sabbath, entered the Italian ritual itself — still sung when the entry was written. The bibliography is long for so short a notice, running from Steinschneider to Mortara.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motot-simeon-be:
Simeon ben Moses ben Simeon Motot was a Jewish mathematician of the fifteenth century, probably in Lombardy. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and Max Schloessinger, admits that nothing is known of his life. His date is guessed from the friends to whom he dedicated his algebra. They flourished at Mantua in the middle of the century.

Two small works of his survive. His Sefer ha-Alzibra takes a Christian book of theorems stated without proof and supplies the missing demonstrations, adding theorems of his own. The other work solves the problem of the asymptotes, the two lines that approach but never meet. Later scholars credit him with the pure equations of the third and fourth degrees.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahmoli-joseph-: Joseph Nahmoli was an eighteenth-century Talmudist and rabbi of Larissa, given a short notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia by its editorial committee and J. S. Raisin. He had studied under Hayyim Abulafia. His son-in-law was Isaac ibn Shangi, author of a commentary on the Pentateuch. Nahmoli himself wrote homilies for Sabbaths and holy days, printed at Smyrna, and another work issued with his teacher's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naumbourg-samue:
Samuel Naumbourg was a French composer of synagogue music. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Dennenlohe, Bavaria, on March 15, 1817. He died at Saint-Mandé, near Paris, on May 1, 1880. He first served as hazzan at Besançon.

Naumbourg directed the choir at Strasburg after Besançon. In 1845 Paris called him to the Nazareth synagogue. He also taught liturgical music at the Séminaire Israélite. His Chants Liturgicals appeared in 1847. Zemirot Yisrael, in 1864, held the complete liturgy in music. His last work revived songs by Solomon de Rossi. Baron Edmond de Rothschild had found part of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nevakhovich-lob:
Löb Nevakhovich was a Russian writer who defended his people. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Letichev, Volhynia, in the 1700s. He died at St. Petersburg in August 1831. He went there young under Abram Peretz's patronage.

Trade came first, then literature won him over. He was among Russia's first Jews fluent in Russian. He loved Mendelssohn and took pride in Russian patriotism. His Cry of the Daughter of Judah pled for tolerance. It was a Russian Jew's first public defense of Jews. His play Sulioty reached the Imperial Theater in 1809. The emperor himself saw it performed that October. His grandson was the scientist Mechnikov of later fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-norden-joshua-d:
Joshua D. Norden was an English soldier and adventurer. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Graham's Town in Cape Colony. The date was April 26, in 1846. He held a captain's rank in the yeomanry.

He was field commandant in the Kaffir war then. In 1846 he led mounted men against the Kaffirs. Six men rode with him toward the hills. The enemy lay in ambush along their path. A rifle ball pierced Norden's head in the fight. His men were forced to retire without him. Next day they recovered their commandant's body. It was found in a shockingly mutilated state. The Jewish Chronicle reported his death that July.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olive-11686:
The olive is a green tree that keeps its leaves all year. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is one of the most marked trees of Palestine. The Hebrew word zayit names the grown, tame tree. A wild kind grew in the land as well.

No one can say just where the olive first grew wild. Its use in Egypt and Syria goes far back. In Palestine it was grown long before Israel came. The Canaanites taught the new folk how to raise it. A branch of it comes in the tale of Noah's ark. The tree is grown from wild stocks that are grafted. The soil round it must be plowed more than once a year. Its fruit is picked in the fall months.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osiris-daniel-1:
Daniel Osiris was a French giver of gifts and patron of art. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bordeaux on July 23, 1825. For more than half a century he knew great men. Those men led in art, in rule, in books, and in science.

Daniel gave his life and his wealth to good works. He gave his home town a set of public springs. At Arcachon he built a fine synagogue for the Jews. He set up a statue of Joan of Arc at Nancy. That town gave him its freedom for the gift. He built a Paris synagogue in the Rue Buffault. It was opened on September 3, in 1877. In 1903 he gave the state the famed Malmaison house. That house had been the home of the empress Josephine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-panzieri-or-pan:
Panzieri was a Portuguese family found in two great towns. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its men are met at Constantinople and at Rome. They are met there from the sixteen hundreds on. The family still had men in Italy in 1904.

The chief man of the Constantinople branch was Ephraim Panzieri. He was a doctor and a man of the Cabala school. He thrived at Constantinople about the year 1550. He went to Damascus to read with Hayyim Vital there. He lived a strict life of fast and prayer in that town. Men held him in awe and called him a saint. The Rome branch held Moses and Shabbethai Panzieri. Shabbethai was rabbi of Rome in 1652 and 1653.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-de-toledo:
Pedro de Toledo was Spain's viceroy in Naples. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He stood out as a friend and protector of Jews. Few rulers of his age earned that name. His court gave Jews room to serve and teach.

About 1530 he took Don Samuel Abravanel into his service. Samuel, the youngest son of Isaac Abravanel, ran his finances. The viceroy's daughter Leonora also crossed the usual lines. She took lessons from Samuel's wife, the learned Benvenida. Leonora later married Cosimo de Medici of Florence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pharaoh-lxx-120:
Pharaoh is the Bible's title for the kings of Egypt. Emil G. Hirsch and Louis H. Gray wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word starts as Egyptian for great house. It first named the palace, not the king.

The meaning shifted slowly from house to ruler. By the eighteenth dynasty it named the monarch outright. The Bible speaks of eleven Egyptian kings in all. The first took Sarai into his harem in error. He freed her when God struck his house. Joseph's Pharaoh gets a close look at names and dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pirogov-nikolai:
Nikolai Pirogov was a Russian surgeon and school reformer. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1810 and died in 1881. His fame in medicine reached across Russia.

Alexander the Second sought Pirogov's counsel on schools. He made him superintendent at Odessa, then at Kiev. There Pirogov first came to know the Jews. He treated them with rare and open fairness. Class prejudice, he said, had no place in science. His farewell to Berdychev's Jews disclaimed all credit. Fairness, he told them, was simply his nature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porges-nathan-1:
Nathan Porges was a German rabbi born at Prossnitz in Moravia in 1848. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Olmütz and then at Breslau. He took a doctorate and his rabbi's title there in 1869. A long string of pulpits followed.

Porges served at Nakel from 1875 and Mannheim from 1879. He moved to Pilsen in 1880 and Carlsbad in 1882. Since 1888 he has served at Leipsic. He wrote many essays and reviews for learned journals. French and German journals of Jewish study printed his work. He wrote most often on old Hebrew books and their past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-of-parzi: Rabbah of Parziki was a Babylonian teacher of the sixth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the same time as Ashi, the great editor. He held talks with Ashi again and again. Three tractates of the Talmud name those talks. His learned son Huna was a pupil of Ashi too. No work or saying of his own is set down.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-robert-of-bury-: Robert of Bury St. Edmunds was an alleged martyr of a blood accusation. Joseph Jacobs wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. The accusation was made at Bury St. Edmunds in Suffolk, England, in 1181. No details are known of how he was made a martyr. The Jews of Bury were expelled ten years later. That expulsion was doubtless linked to the accusation, the entry says. Jacobs's Jews of Angevin England is the cited source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosewater-victo:
Victor Rosewater was an American editor and economist born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1871. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A son of Edward Rosewater, he took two degrees at Columbia University.

Rosewater earned his doctorate at Columbia in 1893, at about twenty-two. That same year he joined the staff of his father's Omaha Bee. Within two years he was the paper's managing editor. In 1896 he became a regent of the Nebraska State University. His book Special Assessments studies how cities finance local public works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-abba: Samuel ben Abbahu was a Babylonian amora of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He is known for one ritual dispute, over eating the Circassian goat as food. Samuel was ready to permit it, while R. Ahai opposed him on the point. The question was sent to Palestine for a ruling at last. The answer came back in Samuel's favor, as Hullin records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanua-james-cal:
Isidore Singer and Richard Gottheil wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on James Sanua. He was an Egyptian publicist, born at Cairo in April 1839. Egyptians called him Abu Naddara, the man with the spectacles. He studied in Egypt and in Italy. At sixteen he was already writing for newspapers in four languages. In 1863 he became a professor at the Ecole Polytechnique in Cairo.

In 1870 Sanua brought the modern Arabic theater to Egypt. He wrote thirty-two plays and translated many more. In 1877 he founded his journal, Le Journal d'Abou Naddara. In it he foretold the English invasion of Egypt. His attacks on the government brought exile in 1878. From Paris he kept publishing his fiercely anti-English paper. In 1900 the Shah of Persia named him Poet of the Empire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schmid-anton-vo:
Joseph Jacobs and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Anton von Schmid. He was a Christian publisher of Hebrew books. Schmid was born at Zwettl, in Lower Austria, on January 23, 1765. He died at Vienna on June 27, 1855. His father meant him for the clergy. Anton left that path and apprenticed under the court printer Kurzbeck in 1785.

At the Oriental academy, Schmid learned Hebrew typesetting and loved it. Rival printers blocked his license to print. He petitioned Emperor Francis the Second directly. The emperor granted the privilege, asking one copy of each book for the imperial library. Schmid soon bought Kurzbeck's whole establishment. By 1816 he had given the library 200 volumes. The emperor answered with a gold medal. Later gifts earned him a title of nobility. His press issued the Talmud, Maimonides, and the Biur Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shakna-shalom-c:
Shalom Shakna, usually called Shakna ben Joseph, was a Polish Talmudist born about 1510. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Bernhard Friedberg wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He learned from Jacob Pollak, founder of the pilpul method of study. By 1528 Shakna already drew hundreds to his Lublin school.

His pupils became leading rabbis across Poland and beyond. One, Moses Isserles of Cracow, married Shakna's daughter. On his deathbed in 1558, Shakna barred his son from printing his manuscripts. He acted, the entry says, from extreme modesty. One early treatise of his did reach print. The entry honors a teacher whose influence ran through students, not books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shir-ha-shirim-:
Shir ha-Shirim Zuta is a smaller homiletic commentary on Canticles, the Song of Songs. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Old collections quote it as Midrash Shir ha-Shirim. A Parma manuscript brought it back to modern readers.

S. Buber found that manuscript holding midrashim on four scrolls. They covered Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, and Ecclesiastes. He printed them in 1894 as Midrash Zuta, the lesser midrash. Schechter issued the Canticles part alone soon after. Zuta does not resemble the larger Rabbah at all. It has no opening proems and treats verses unevenly. Some verses get long treatment, others a single word. The entry contrasts two ways rabbis read one love poem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-boethu:
Simeon ben Boethus was the first high priest of the Boethus family in Jerusalem's Temple. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was a native of Alexandria in Egypt. His rise came through his daughter Mariamne's beauty.

Mariamne captivated King Herod with her looks and charm. Herod raised her father to give her fitting rank. He then took Mariamne as his second wife. When Herod later put that Mariamne away, Simeon fell too. The king deposed him from the high priesthood entirely. The entry shows a priestly office granted and revoked by a king's marriage politics at Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stahl-wilhelm-1:
Wilhelm Stahl was a German economist born at Munich in 1812. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on June 2 of that year. Orphaned young, he was raised in a philologist's home at Erlangen. His brother was Friedrich Julius Stahl, the famed jurist.

He studied at Munich and Halle, focusing on physics and chemistry. He taught at the industrial school in Fürth for a time. Professor Hermann urged him toward political economy as a field. He became a docent and then professor at Erlangen. In 1848 he sat in the Frankfort Parliament for his district. From 1851 he taught at Giessen until his death in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strousberg-beth:
Bethel Henry Strousberg was a German railway contractor born in 1823. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Neidenburg, East Prussia, on November 20. After failing in London business he emigrated to America. He died at Berlin on June 1, 1884.

Strousberg taught languages at New Orleans for a time. Back in London he traded in damaged goods and publishing. In 1861 he won an East Prussian railway concession. He then built lines across Germany, Hungary, and Rumania. At his peak he employed over 100,000 people. His schemes involved nearly one hundred million pounds. War losses and a Rumanian settlement ruined him. Bankruptcy came in 1875 after a Russian fraud trial. The entry tells a spectacular rise and collapse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tabi-14186:
Tabi was the slave of Gamaliel the Second in rabbinic tradition. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. The Mishnah mentions him in several places. He was known for learning and piety alike. That pairing made him stand out among slaves.

During Tabernacles, Tabi slept under the bed in the booth. Gamaliel praised him for knowing slaves were exempt. Yet Tabi wore phylacteries, a free man's duty and privilege. His piety was so known that none stopped him. Gamaliel once hoped an injury had freed him by law. Rabbi Joshua showed the freeing failed for lack of witnesses. When Tabi died, friends condoled with his master. The entry honors a slave honored as a scholar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiberias-14386:
Tiberias, a Galilean city on Lake Gennesaret, was founded by Herod Antipas. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Herod built it in 26 C.E. He named it for the emperor Tiberius. Hot springs lay near its beautiful shore.

Bones found during building made the site seem unclean. Pious Jews shunned a city built on graves. Herod had to lure beggars and foreigners to settle it. Some settlers came only under force. Still, most residents were Jews in the end. A council of five hundred governed the city. Ten elders levied its taxes. In 66 the town split into three factions over revolt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trani-10886:
Trani was a family of scholars prominent in Spain and the Levant. Marcus Jastrow, Louis Ginzberg, and Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Aaron di Trani, a Spanish tosafist, heads the entry. He studied under R. Joseph Alfasi's line. In 1502 he reached Adrianople.

At Adrianople Aaron met Joseph Caro, then publishing Bet Yosef. Contemporaries esteemed Aaron highly as a Talmudist. He championed pilpul, the sharp analytic method. His nephew Moses carried pilpul into Palestine's schools. Joseph di Trani, an uncle of Moses, settled at Salonica in 1502. Another Joseph, the Elder, won fame for vast responsa. His three-part collection holds hundreds of rulings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-travnik-14486:
Travnik, a town in Bosnia, gained its first Jews early in the 1800s. Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Wessel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Most newcomers were Sephardim from Sarajevo. An army purveyor, an army surgeon, and a rabbi led the way. A Belgrade Jew collected the town's taxes for the Ottomans.

Ottoman officials let Jewish tax staff close on feast days. Around 1840 the growing community built a wooden chapel. A massive temple replaced it in 1863. Leading Jews carried stone and brick for the work themselves. A schoolhouse followed in 1877. Fire destroyed both buildings in 1903. The town's 426 Jews had never faced persecution there. They lived at peace with all other creeds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vesoul-hebr-or-:
Vesoul is a French town, capital of Haute Saône. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there in the late twelve hundreds. Their leader was Hayyim ben Jacob, a rabbinic correspondent. The synagogue stood inside the city walls.

In 1315 a Vesoul banker named Héliot helped negotiate. He worked for the return of Jews expelled from France. Three years later a countess seized a local Jew's house. In 1321 the Jews of Vesoul were expelled. The synagogue was sold for the public treasury. In 1348 eighty local Jews faced a well poisoning charge. The entry records loss after loss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-washing-14786:
Washing held a religious role in ancient Hebrew life. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Water was scarce in the land, so baths were rare. Ritual rules gave cleanliness a sacred basis instead. People washed before meals by custom. Water stood at the heart of the cult.

Springs and rivers held divine meaning for Semites. To wash in them was itself a ritual act. No one could approach God while unclean. Worshippers washed their bodies and their clothes. The camp of Israel counted as holy ground. The entry explains how purity rules grew from these roots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wheat-hebr-hitt:
Wheat was the chief bread grain of ancient Palestine. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word is hittah. Growing wheat marks a higher stage than barley alone. Barley bread served the common people. Wheat loaves served at sacrifice used the choicest flour.

Farmers sow wheat in late autumn, after early rains. The harvest runs from late April into June. It falls somewhat later than the barley harvest. Tyre bought wheat from Judah in Bible times. Galilee was famed as the most fruitful district. The Hauran still serves as Syria's great granary. Roasted grains were also eaten as food.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-aaron-149:
Aaron Wolff (1795-1872) was a Danish merchant who held high posts on Saint Thomas. Joseph Jacobs and Lilian N. Levy wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born on Saint Christopher, he came from the Fonseca kin line. Soon after 1814 he moved to Saint Thomas in the Danish West Indies.

There he rose to the post of town chief, next to the governor. The King of Denmark gave him a high order of merit. He sat on the Royal Council of the island. For thirty-two years he ran the Bank of Saint Thomas. He also led its marine firms and its synagogue for years. Before the king freed the slaves in 1843, Wolff freed his own. That act stands out in the short entry on his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yezirah-sefer-b:
Sefer Yezirah, or Book of Creation, is the name of two deep books. Kaufmann Kohler and Louis Ginzberg wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The older book is also called Rules of Creation. It is a work of wonders prized in Talmud days.

One tale tells of two pupils of Rabbi Judah the Prince. On each eve of the Sabbath they made a young calf. They made it by the book and ate it that night. A sage says no witch craft was used in that act. The work was done by the signs of the Holy Name. A like tale is told of the man who built the tent shrine. He worked by the same play of signs, men said. Gnostic groups held like books in the old world too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yigdal-15086:
Yigdal is a hymn sung at dawn prayer and at night's close. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It shares that place of honor with Adon Olam. It rests on the thirteen rules of faith of Maimonides. A judge named Daniel ben Judah wrote the hymn.

He spent eight years to hone the hymn to its form. He brought it to its end in the year 1404. More than one verse form of the rules was made. This one outlived all the rest in use by far. Jews of the north sing thirteen lines of the hymn. One line stands for each rule of the faith. The last line, on the rise of the dead, is sung twice. Jews of the south sing one more line to close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zacuto-moses-be:
Moses ben Mordecai Zacuto (born about 1625) was a cabalist and poet. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Mantua in the year 1697. Men think he was born at Amsterdam in the north.

He may have lived at Venice in his youth as well. His teacher there died, and he wrote a long dirge for him. He was a school mate of Baruch Spinoza in those days. From his youth he leaned to the mystic path in faith. Once he fasted forty days to lose his Latin tongue. He held that tongue at odds with cabalist truth then. He went east to Posen to press his Talmud work. In time he served as rabbi at Venice for long years. He left that post in 1673 for a call to Mantua.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebahim-animal-:
Zebahim is the tract on the laws of beast gifts to God. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and the Babylon Talmud. In the Tosefta its name is Korbanot, or Gifts in tongue.

Its old name in the Talmud is Slaughter of Holy Things. It is the first tract in the order of holy things. It has fourteen parts with one hundred one rules in all. Part one treats the aim that must guide a gift rite. The Passover gift must be slain at its set time. Part two treats what makes a gift unfit for the altar. It treats the foul state called piggul in the law. A gift turns piggul by a wrong aim in its rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zucker-alfred-1:
Alfred Zucker was a German chemist and maker of chemical products at Dresden. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Zucker was born in Uffenheim, Bavaria, on August 17, 1871. He studied pharmacy and chemistry at the universities of Würzburg and Erlangen.

While still a student, Zucker joined a government commission fighting a vine pest that destroyed grapes. His work helped bring that fight to success. He later served as military apothecary at the Bavarian home for pensioned soldiers. His books treat a copper spray used on plants and the chemistry of photography. He also wrote short pharmacy studies that drew notice from specialists.
kural-pope-1886:
G. U. Pope gave English its first complete Tirukkural in 1886, The Sacred Kurral of Tiruvalluva-Nayanar, a work of years. Tiruvalluvar's Tamil classic packs a whole ethics into 1,330 short couplets, each just a few words long. Virtue, wealth, and love, aram, porul, and inbam in Tamil, divide the book's three great sections in order.

Kings and farmers alike have quoted the Kural for centuries as a guide to living well in this world. Pope, a missionary-scholar who loved Tamil deeply, labored to carry its terse wisdom whole into English verse. His version opened one of world literature's most treasured short works to the West at last.
lafontaine-fables-thornbury-1886:
Animals talk sense in La Fontaine's Fables, and Walter Thornbury's verse translation of 1886 gives all twelve books complete. The Grasshopper and the Ant opens a parade of foxes, wolves, lions, and lambs. Each short tale ends in a point about power, folly, or kindness that lands without preaching.

La Fontaine borrowed old plots from Aesop and others, then made them French art. Courts and peasants alike quoted him, and children have learned him by heart ever since. Thornbury's rhymes keep the snap of the originals, so English readers get both the story and the sting.
le-plongeon-sacred-mysteries-1886:
Augustus Le Plongeon dug among Maya ruins and came back with a lost continent in 1886. Sacred Mysteries Among the Mayas and the Quiches, 11,500 Years Ago ties the stones of Yucatan to deep time. Le Plongeon gave the lost land its famed name: Mu.

He held that Maya priests kept rites and records passed down from Mu, and that Egypt drew its own lore from the same source. Donnelly and Churchward later built on his claims. His readings of the stones were bold, and scholars have set most of them aside. The book stays prized as the eccentric root of a whole line of thought.
les-fables-egyptiennes-et-grecques-devoi: Antoine-Joseph Pernety published the first volume of his Egyptian and Greek Fables in 1786. The hosted sample shows little beyond the title page. His subtitle promises to unveil those fables. Pernety reduces the myths to one shared principle, he claims. He also explains hieroglyphs, the picture writing of Egypt. His reading treats old gods' tales as coded alchemy.

The second volume of Pernety's Egyptian and Greek Fables appeared in 1786. Its title page repeats his long promise. Fables are unveiled and reduced to one principle. An explanation of hieroglyphs accompanies that argument. Pernety reads Greek and Egyptian myths as veiled natural doctrine. This volume completes his two-part case from 1786.
lotze-outlines-aesthetics-1886:
Hermann Lotze's Outlines of Aesthetics reached English readers in George Ladd's translation of 1886. Lotze, a professor at Göttingen, had lectured on beauty and art as part of his wider system of philosophy. The Outlines series, drawn from his lecture courses, gave students his thought in brief compass.

Lotze treats art as the meeting of spirit and sense: beauty is the form in which feeling recognizes value in the world of the senses. He works through the fine arts and the nature of taste without dryness or jargon for its own sake. Ladd, a Yale philosopher, carried the lectures to American classrooms. The book is often called the German master's swan song in English dress. It stands as one of the most humane works on aesthetics that the nineteenth century produced.
lotze-outlines-psychology-1886:
Ladd's translation of Lotze's Outlines of Psychology appeared in 1886. Lotze was trained as both doctor and philosopher, a rare pairing that shaped his study of the mind. In his century, psychology still lived inside philosophy's house. Lotze's lectures were a leading attempt to map the soul before the science moved out on its own.

The Outlines cover sensation, feeling, memory, and thought, asking how the mind builds a world from the body's signals. Lotze resists reducing the soul to machinery while honoring the facts of physiology. His account of how we locate things in space was widely discussed. The book gives the German master's study of the soul in brief, careful form. It remains a fine record of mind-science at the moment before experimental psychology took over the field.
man-and-wife-pg1586:
Wilkie Collins opens Man and Wife with two girls weeping in a ship's cabin. Blanche and Anne are eighteen, bound outward from Gravesend to Bombay. They have been close friends and pupil-teachers at the same school. Now they part, perhaps for life, to earn their own bread.

Blanche is pleasant and ordinary; Anne is beautiful and rarely gifted. A prologue on an Irish marriage frames their later troubles. Collins spins their fates into a trap of marriage law. A secret union and a villain's denial put Anne in peril. The novel mixes sensation plotting with real legal reform. It shows Collins at the height of his powers.
manu-smriti-buhler-1886:
The Laws of Manu appear here in Georg Bühler's English translation. It forms volume twenty-five of the Sacred Books of the East. F. Max Müller edited that series at the Clarendon Press. Bühler adds extracts from seven old commentaries on the text.

The Laws of Manu are ancient India's great code of duty. They order caste, marriage, kingship, penance, and daily conduct. Priests, warriors, farmers, and servants each receive their rules. Few books have shaped a civilization's life so deeply. Bühler's version, printed in 1886, became the standard English text. Students of religion and law still consult it today.
marx-wage-labour-capital-joynes-1886:
Marx lectured on wages in Brussels in December 1847, and those talks became Wage-Labour and Capital. J. L. Joynes gave the work its first English translation in London in 1886. The Modern Press published that edition. Marx explains what wages are and what capital is, in terms workers could follow.

He argues that labour itself becomes a commodity bought and sold. Capital grows, on his account, from the unpaid part of the worker's day. The short work holds the seed of the first volume of Capital. Its plain style made it a staple of worker education. Readers meet Marx the teacher here. The argument stays clear throughout.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume three of Campan's memoirs opens at chapter six, at a new reign. Louis XVI spends his first months at La Muette, Marly, and Compiegne. At Versailles he pores over his grandfather's papers for secrets.

He hunts in vain for proof on the man with the iron mask. Maurepas tells him the man was a Mantuan subject, lured and seized. He was held at Pignerol, then moved to the Bastille with his keeper. Campan says the public still chose Voltaire's grand tale over that plain truth. A velvet mask worn against the sun may have seeded the tale. Campan weighs fact and fable with a courtier's care here.
mommsen-provinces-roman-empire-1886:
Theodor Mommsen's The Provinces of the Roman Empire appears here in William P. Dickson's translation of 1886. The book is Mommsen's sequel on the Empire from Caesar to Diocletian. He surveys the provinces one by one: Spain, Gaul, Britain, the Danube lands, Greece, Asia, Syria, and Egypt. Administration, armies, cities, and local cultures fill the account.

Mommsen shows an empire held together by law, roads, and Roman citizenship. His knowledge of inscriptions gives the survey unmatched depth. The work lacks the narrative fire of the Republic volumes, by design. It is a handbook of genius rather than a story. Students of Rome still mine it today.
openalex-w2077384386:
Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration reported first results on three particle types from lead collisions. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in 2012. The particles were pions, kaons and protons. Their patterns reveal how the hot collision matter expands. The collisions happened at the Large Hadron Collider.

The team measured particle yields at mid-rapidity. They compared results with earlier lower-energy data. The patterns showed much stronger outward flow. Dense matter pushes particles out as it expands. One particle ratio matched thermal model predictions well. Another ratio came out clearly lower than expected. That mismatch remains unexplained, the authors note. The data sharpen models of quark-gluon plasma.
openalex-w2102728586:
Justin Pulford, Manuel Hetzel, Miranda Bryant and colleagues reviewed why people skip mosquito nets they own. Their paper appeared in Malaria Journal in 2011. Nets protect against malaria when used nightly. Many owners still sleep without them sometimes. Programmes needed a summary of the stated reasons.

The team searched the medical literature systematically. They included studies that recorded owners' own reasons. Twenty-two studies met their criteria. Heat discomfort was the most common reason given. Low perceived mosquito numbers came next. Other reasons included net condition and sleeping arrangements. Knowing real reasons can shape better promotion. Comfort improvements may raise nightly use.
openalex-w2108080286:
Adriane Ribeiro Rosa, Jose Sanchez-Moreno, Anabel Martinez-Aran and colleagues tested a short functioning scale for bipolar disorder. Their paper appeared in 2007. Bipolar patients often struggle with daily functioning. Problems persist even between mood episodes. Existing tools measured functioning only in broad terms.

The new test, called FAST, covers several life areas. It asks about work, relationships and daily skills. Patients in different mood states completed it. Scores separated patients from healthy comparisons clearly. The scale agreed well with other functioning measures. Repeated testing gave consistent results. Clinicians gained a quick, focused assessment tool. It suits both practice and treatment studies.
openalex-w2127938786:
René Garreaud wrote this review alone in Advances in Geosciences in 2009. He sets out the main features of weather and climate over the Andes, the long mountain chain along the west of South America. The account rests on instrument records rather than models alone.

Garreaud first explains the yearly cycle of winds and rain over the range and nearby lowlands. The chain is so long and high that it blocks large air flows and creates sharp contrasts between slopes. Rain, temperature, and wind patterns differ strongly from place to place. He also documents how the El Niño Southern Oscillation shifts temperature and rainfall regimes along the Andes.
openalex-w2143675486:
Wendy Snowdon, Astika Raj, Erica Reeve, and colleagues published this study in Globalization and Health in 2013. They built a dataset on the nutrient content of processed foods sold in the Pacific Islands. Island nations rely heavily on imported food, yet food tables say little about these packaged products.

Shoppers recorded label data in large stores in Fiji, Guam, Nauru, New Caledonia, and Samoa. The dataset holds over six thousand foods and drinks from fifty-four countries of origin. Each island's main supplier was the country it was most strongly linked to politically. Some labels lacked nutrient data, over a hundred were inaccurate, and more than a quarter carried health-related claims.
openalex-w2152546486:
Oumar Faye, Caio Freire, Atila Iamarino, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014. They traced the molecular evolution of Zika virus during its twentieth-century emergence. The mosquito-borne virus was first isolated in Uganda in 1947, yet few human cases were reported before a 2007 epidemic in Micronesia.

The team studied thirty-seven virus isolates gathered from 1968 to 2002 in Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire. Strains from six other countries were added for comparison. Their results suggest West Africa saw at least two separate introductions of the virus in that century. The lineages were apparently not restricted to particular mosquito species, which helps explain the virus's quiet spread.
openalex-w2234243486:
S. Chatrchyan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this study in Physical Review C in 2011. They observed jet quenching in lead-lead collisions, where jets lose energy plowing through the hot matter the collision creates. Jets are rebuilt from energy dumped in the CMS calorimeters, and paired back-to-back jets make energy loss easy to spot.

With more central collisions, a striking imbalance grew between the two jets of a pair. One jet kept its energy while its partner came out weakened, just as quenching predicts. The effect reached down to the lowest jet energies the study used. The pattern gives direct evidence that the dense medium drains fast partons, a key property physicists use jets to probe.
openalex-w2290750286:
Gloria Lozano, Helena Trenado, and Elvira Fiallo-Olivé led this 2016 study in Frontiers in Microbiology. They describe small DNA satellites found with sweepoviruses, a group of begomoviruses that infect plants. Satellites are tiny hitchhikers. They carry no tools to copy themselves and rely fully on a helper virus in the same plant.

Some known classes carry a gene for a coat protein. The beta satellites make plant disease worse. The ones studied here code for nothing at all, like the first DNA satellite found with a tomato virus in Australia. By comparing their DNA codes and traits, the authors set them apart as a distinct class of begomovirus satellites.
openalex-w2345599686:
Liisa Pelttari, Sofia Khan, Mikko Vuorela, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2016. They investigated the RAD51B gene in familial breast cancer. Common DNA variants near this gene were already tied to breast cancer risk. But damaging mutations in the gene itself were uncharted.

The team sequenced the gene's coding region in Finnish patients from cancer families. One possibly harmful mutation turned up, then was tested in thousands more Finnish and Belarusian cases and controls. It showed no real link to risk. The known common variants, however, replicated strongly, including in familial cases. A haplotype carrying all three risk variants raised familial risk by about a quarter. Damaging RAD51B mutations, they conclude, are rare; common variation matters.
openalex-w2400322086:
Patrícia Izar published this review in Revista de Antropologia in 1995. It examines Evolutionary Ecology and Human Behavior, edited by Eric Alden Smith and Bruce Winterhalder. The book gathers work applying evolution and ecology to human behavior, a young field when she wrote. Natural selection, she explains, was being used to study adaptation in ecological settings, first in animals, then in people.

The editors argue this lens can unify social and evolutionary accounts of behavior. Human choices look rational and goal-driven, yet preferences and beliefs themselves need an evolutionary explanation. One chapter, by Richerson and Boyd, treats cultural evolution as a Darwinian process driven by learning and imitation rather than genes. Izar's review, in Portuguese, maps the young field's ambitions for Brazilian readers.
openalex-w2558185986:
The ATLAS Collaboration published this performance report in the European Physical Journal C in 2017. It describes the ATLAS trigger system, which picks which particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider are worth recording. In 2015 ATLAS gathered proton-proton data at a record energy of thirteen TeV. The trigger had to choose about one thousand events per second from up to forty million collisions.

The paper first explains changes made to the trigger and data systems during the LHC's long shutdown. It then walks through the trigger menu, the set of selection rules used in 2015. Performance results cover the high-level trigger's tracking and calorimeter reconstruction. Timing and processing limits get detailed attention as well. The report confirms the upgraded system handled the tougher Run 2 conditions. It serves as the reference record for how ATLAS selected its 2015 physics data.
openalex-w2989910886:
S. Acharya, D. Adamová, S. P. Adhya, and colleagues of the ALICE collaboration published this paper in Physical Review C in 2020. It measures how many charged pions, kaons, and protons emerge from lead-lead and proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Such collisions briefly create quark-gluon plasma, matter as it was just after the Big Bang.

The ALICE team counted these particles at mid-rapidity across a wide range of speeds. In lead-lead collisions, the counts are sorted by how head-on each collision was. Comparing particle ratios between collision types reveals how the hot plasma expands and cools into ordinary matter. The results test the picture of a thermal, balanced origin for the particles produced.
openalex-w4280552086: Anubha Mahajan, Cassandra Spracklen, Weihua Zhang, and colleagues carried out a multi-ancestry genetic study of type 2 diabetes. Their paper appeared in Nature Genetics in 2022, and its title stresses the power of diverse populations for discovery. The preserved sample holds only the long author list from the article's opening pages. It has no readable abstract or results, so the study's findings cannot be described from it here.
openalex-w7204858686: After the Rio Doce mining disaster, a teacher-training course asked educators to turn the tragedy into lessons. This article studies a teaching product built in that course at a public school in Caratinga, Minas Gerais, and what the training added to teaching about mining. The authors assess how the experience shaped classroom practice. Education as repair work in a community still living with the damage.
phrenology-made-easy-a-new-system-of-men: Phrenology Made Easy, 1886. The easy system. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
plos-pbio-0020086:
Lev Z. Osherovich, Brian S. Cox, Mick F. Tuite, and their group reviewed yeast prions in PLOS Biology in 2004. Prions are proteins that can fold into a shape that copies itself, passing traits down without any change in DNA. In yeast they are easier to study than the prions that cause brain disease in mammals.

The authors take prions apart, step by step, and discuss how to design and test new ones. That dissection shows what a protein needs to act as a prion. Yeast prions are also a safe model for the folding rules behind diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The paper serves as both a guide to the field and a plan for future experiments.
plos-pbio-0020286:
Joshua M. Akey, Michael A. Eberle, Mark J. Rieder, and a large team surveyed human genetic variation in PLOS Biology in 2004. They read 132 genes in people from different populations. Patterns in the data carry marks of both population history and natural selection.

Sorting those two forces apart is a central task in human genetics. History alone can mimic the marks of selection, so careless claims are common. The team's data set gives a broad baseline for telling them apart. Genes that still stand out after that check are strong candidates for real adaptation. Such genes can reveal how human groups adjusted to local diets, climates, and diseases.
plos-pone-0000086:
Christian Beste, Carsten Saft, and Jürgen Andrich studied error handling in Huntington's disease in PLOS ONE in 2006. Huntington's is a brain disorder that harms movement, thought, and feeling. When healthy people make an error, brain systems react at once to adjust. The team measured that error response in patients.

Faulty error processing can explain part of the clumsiness and poor learning seen in the disease. If the brain does not flag its own mistakes well, correction lags. The measures used here are sensitive and quick, so they may track disease progress or treatment effects. The study shows a mental fault that standard exams can miss, adding depth to how Huntington's is assessed.
plos-pone-0000186:
David Méary, Elenitsa Kitromilides, Karine Mazens, and colleagues published this infant perception study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Newborns just four days old were shown a single point of light in motion. The babies looked longer at non-biological motions than at the smooth motion of a living thing.

From the first days of life, infants react differently to how things move. Looking-time studies are the main window into what a newborn's mind registers. This result was surprising because older infants and adults usually favor biological motion; the paper refines the timeline of how that preference develops.
plos-pone-0000286:
Ryosuke Kimura, Akihiro Fujimoto, Katsushi Tokunaga, and colleagues published this population genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. A selective sweep happens when a helpful gene variant spreads so fast it fixes, becoming universal in a population, and drags nearby DNA with it. The authors present a practical genome scan for strong sweeps that reached fixation in specific populations.

Fixed sweeps mark places where populations adapted hard to local conditions, such as diet or climate. A practical scan helps find them without false alarms. The method serves the study of recent human evolution, where such sweeps are key evidence.
plos-pone-0000386:
Michael Opel and colleagues mapped a genome-wide chemical process in fission yeast, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Histones are the spool proteins DNA wraps around, and removing methyl tags from them changes which genes are active. The team studied yeast versions of the mammal enzyme LSD1, a known histone demethylase.

By tracking demethylation across the whole genome, the study shows where these enzymes act and which genes they free up or shut down. Yeast is far simpler than a mammal, so its version of the machinery exposes the basic rules. Those rules matter because faulty histone marking is linked to cancer and other diseases in humans.
plos-pone-0000486:
Giovanni Frazzetto and colleagues asked how early hardship and one gene together shape adult aggression, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is MAOA, which breaks down brain signaling chemicals and has been linked to impulsive behavior. The team studied early trauma and the risk for physical aggression during adulthood, testing whether MAOA genotype moderates that risk.

Moderation means the trauma's effect depends on which gene version a person carries. Studies of this kind try to explain why similar childhoods lead to very different adults. They are also watched closely for misuse, since a gene is a risk factor, never a verdict on any individual.
plos-pone-0000586:
Yalei Wu and colleagues studied how loss of estrogen reshapes bone through immune-style signals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The signals run through ITAM adapters, parts that immune cells use to pass messages. Bone is always being rebuilt, in a cycle of removal and renewal. The team asked what these adapters do inside bone's own setting when estrogen drops fast.

When estrogen falls, removal outruns renewal and bones thin, the state called osteoporosis. Showing that immune-style signals act right inside bone sharpens that picture. It also hints that the immune system and the skeleton share control parts. Drugs might one day use those parts to guard bone.
plos-pone-0000686:
Rhys E. Green, Mark A. Taggart, Kalu Ram Senacha and colleagues estimated how fast India's white-backed vultures were vanishing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The painkiller diclofenac is a major cause of rapid declines in three vulture species native to South Asia. It causes kidney failure and death in the birds. Exposure likely comes when vultures feed on carcasses of treated livestock.

To measure decline, the team surveyed diclofenac residues in carcasses of ungulates, hoofed animals, across India. Residue levels in the birds' food supply feed a model of population loss. Vultures clean landscapes of carrion, so their collapse carries public health costs as well.
plos-pone-0000786:
Israel Pagán, Carlos Alonso-Blanco and Fernando García-Arenal tested a basic assumption about why parasites harm their hosts, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Virulence, the damage a parasite does, offers the parasite no obvious advantage. Most models of virulence evolution assume the damage is an unavoidable consequence of within-host multiplication, traded off against transmission between hosts. More growth means more transmission, but also more harm.

Their system is a plant virus, where the relationship between multiplication inside a host and virulence can be measured directly. If multiplication and harm do not track together, the standard trade-off model needs revision. Plant systems let evolution theory be tested without the noise of animal immunity.
plos-pone-0000886:
Kimberley Hockings, Tatyana Humle, James Anderson and colleagues reported chimpanzees regularly sharing plant food, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Wild chimpanzees rarely share plant foods with each other. Meat from hunts is shared often, and it works as a social tool for building bonds and alliances.

Against that background, steady sharing of a prized plant food stands out. The authors call it forbidden fruit, picked where taking it carried some risk. Sharing it may have bought social rewards worth that risk. The report adds a plant based case to a debate that has mostly been about meat, status and friendship among apes.
plos-pone-0000986:
Jerker Fick, Richard Lindberg, Mats Tysklind and colleagues found that sewage treatment does not remove the flu drug oseltamivir, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Oseltamivir is the main drug for treating and preventing pandemic flu. Resistance to it had already been rising, raising debate about wide use.

If the drug passes through treatment plants unchanged, it reaches rivers where flu carrying birds gather. Virus exposed to low drug levels there could evolve resistance outside any hospital. The team test what normal sewage treatment does to the drug, and report it is neither removed nor degraded. The finding links pharmacy to ecology in one short chain.
plos-pone-0001086:
Pim van Hooft, Barend Greyling, Herbert Prins and colleagues found strong selection on the buffalo Y chromosome tied to rainfall, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Selection on the mammalian Y chromosome usually stays near neutral, neither helping nor harming much. The Y passes only through males, so its story is a narrow one.
