In two African buffalo populations, the team show strong balancing selection keeping Y variants at intermediate frequencies. Rainfall is the driver they implicate. A climate linked pattern on the Y is unusual and suggests male success swings with wet and dry cycles. Wildlife genetics rarely gets so specific a suspect.
plos-pone-0001186:
Bacteria sense the damaging chemical superoxide and answer by switching genes on and off. Jeffrey Blanchard and colleagues watched that answer unfold over time in E. coli, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The response system is built around two proteins, SoxR and SoxS, which detect superoxide levels inside the cell.

Using a time-series microarray design, the team identified gene networks that respond with the SoxRS system and others that respond independently of it. Gene expression changed rapidly after superoxide exposure. Separating the two networks clarifies how bacteria defend themselves against oxidative stress, a weapon the immune system also uses against them.
plos-pone-0001286:
Classic evolutionary theory predicts that populations facing high rates of death from external causes should age faster. Stephanie Carlson, Ray Hilborn, and Andrew Hendry tested that prediction in wild salmon, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their external cause is predation by bears, which falls unevenly on salmon populations.

The authors report that predation by bears drives senescence in natural populations of salmon. The theory usually neglects how an individual's aged condition affects its chance of being caught; their study accounts for that interplay. Wild populations rarely offer such clean tests of aging theory.
plos-pone-0001386:
Per Erixon and Bengt Oxelman wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene in the green power units of plant cells. Change in plant DNA is often slow, and change that alters proteins is slower still. That is because harmful shifts tend to be weeded out. The pair asked why this one gene breaks that calm pattern.

They show the gene has been under strong push to change across many plant lines. It also shows fast rates for silent changes, plus gene copies and small gains and losses. Such a mix is rare for this genome. The case helps show how one gene can take a swift path while the rest stay slow.
plos-pone-0001486:
Ahmad Khalil and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new RNA found in fragile X syndrome. Most of the genome is copied into RNA, but only a tiny share codes for proteins. The rest was long dismissed, yet much of it has real jobs. The team characterized one such RNA with a cell saving role.

They show this RNA helps keep cells from dying, and that it is silenced in fragile X syndrome. Loss of a saving RNA could add to the harm in that syndrome. The work adds to the fast shift in how labs view non coding RNA. Each new case makes the old junk label harder to hold.
plos-pone-0001586:
Linda Zheng and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on virus hunting tests. Labs spot new viruses with primers, short DNA starts aimed at spots kept the same across kin. Those kept spots are found by lining up known sequences. As more species are found, the kept spots can shrink. The team tracked that effect in one virus family.

They show that species finds drive much of the new variation at kept spots. Primer sets thus age and must be rebuilt as finds grow. Stale primers can miss new viruses in full. The work gives labs a rule for when to refresh their hunting tools.
plos-pone-0001686:
David A. Hughes, Kun Tang, Rainer Strotmann, and their co-authors found signs of parallel natural selection in a human gene in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The gene is TRPV6, a candidate for local directional selection in Europeans. Selection can act on new mutations or on variation already standing in a population.

Using a modified test that looks for long, uniform stretches of DNA around a gene, the authors reach a clear verdict. Selection acted on standing variation at TRPV6. That produced parallel soft sweeps, similar selection events in separate groups. The full text gives the population data and the test results. Soft sweeps from standing variation may be a common way humans adapted to local diets and climates, and TRPV6 gives a worked example.
plos-pone-0001786:
Srinidi Mohan, Peter W. K. Ma, W. Paul Williams, and their co-authors studied a maize protein that poisons caterpillars in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. When caterpillars feed on maize lines with native resistance to several moth pests, a defensive cysteine protease called Mir1-CP rapidly accumulates at the wound site. It inhibits caterpillar growth by attacking and permeabilizing the insect's gut lining.

The team reports that this plant protease has remarkable toxicity against insect pests and synergizes with Bacillus thuringiensis toxin, the widely used Bt insecticide. The full text gives the feeding assays and the combined-effect data. A plant defense that boosts Bt could extend the life of Bt crops as pests evolve resistance.
plos-pone-0001886:
Liwen Chen and colleagues studied how stem cells from bone marrow help wounds heal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. These stem cells were known to speed wound repair, yet the way they do it was barely grasped. The team focused on what the cells give off, rather than on the cells turning into new skin.

They found that factors shed by the stem cells call in macrophages, the immune cells that clean wounds, and cells of the vessel-lining line. Both cell types are key to repair. If shed factors alone can drive much of the gain, future care might use those factors as a drug. That would be a simpler path than transplanting live cells.
plos-pone-0001986:
Larry Cabral, Brad Foley, and Sergey Nuzhdin asked a thorny question about fruit fly contests, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Winning fights and courtship displays should raise fitness, so traits for aggression and display ought to be winnowed by selection. Yet flies still vary a lot in these traits, which is a puzzle.

The team tested whether the payoff of a trait depends on the genotype of the rival. If success trades off across match-ups, they also asked whether sex changes that trade. If no genotype wins everywhere, variety can persist. Work of this kind tests core claims about how selection shapes behavior.
plos-pone-0002086:
Zengli Yu and co-authors studied why some muscles resist wasting in chronic illness, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cachexia is the deep muscle loss that comes with ills such as chronic heart failure. Oxidative muscles, the slow red kind built for endurance, resist it better than the fast glycolytic kind. The molecular reason for that protection was elusive.

The team hypothesized that nitric oxide, a signaling gas, differs by fiber type and does the protecting. As the title states, fiber-type-specific nitric oxide protects oxidative fibers against cachectic stimuli. If the shield can be copied by drugs, wasting might be slowed where it now cannot.
plos-pone-0002186:
Bu-Er Wang, Xi-De Wang, James Ernst, and co-authors studied growth signals in the prostate gland, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Wnt signals guide how embryos form organs and also play a part in several cancers. Their role in the prostate, both as it grows and when tumors form, was not well mapped.

The team showed that Wnt signaling controls the branching growth of the prostate lining during development. They also linked the same signals to the growth of prostate cancer cells. A pathway that both builds the gland and feeds its tumors is a natural place to look for treatments that can slow the disease.
plos-pone-0002286:
Valeria Berno, Larbi Amazit, Cruz Hinojos, and co-authors compared two ways of switching on the estrogen receptor, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The receptor turns genes on when it binds estradiol, the main estrogen, but growth factors can also activate it with no hormone involved. The lab sought to understand how these two modes of action differ.

Using a cell line with a visible enhancer region, they tracked large-scale changes in chromatin packing and in gene activity after each trigger. Estradiol and the growth factor EGF produced distinct patterns over time. The contrast helps explain how one receptor can run different programs in breast tissue and in tumors.
plos-pone-0002386:
A research team led by Ponts reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Nadia Ponts, Jianfeng Yang, Duk-Won Doug Chung, and others. Its subject is deciphering the Ubiquitin-Mediated Pathway in Apicomplexan Parasites: A Potential Strategy to Interfere with Parasite Virulence. Reversible modification of proteins through the attachment of ubiquitin or ubiquitin-like modifiers is an key post-translational regulatory mechanism in eukaryotes.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002486:
Work from Ortega-Gutiérrez and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Silvia Ortega-Gutiérrez, Donmienne Leung, Scott Ficarro, and others. Its subject is targeted Disruption of the PME-1 Gene Causes Loss of Demethylated PP2A and Perinatal Lethality in Mice. Phosphoprotein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), a major serine-threonine protein phosphatase in eukaryotes.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002586:
In 2008, Carwardine and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Josie Carwardine, Kerrie A. Wilson, Matt Watts, and others. Its subject is avoiding Costly Conservation Mistakes: The Importance of Defining Actions and Costs in Spatial Priority Setting. The typical mandate in conservation planning is to identify areas that represent biodiversity targets within the smallest possible area of land or sea.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002686:
Jan Paul Buschdorf led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was nerve growth factor stimulates interaction of cayman ataxia protein BNIP-H/Caytaxin with Peptidyl-Prolyl isomerase pin1 in differentiating neurons. The catalog record names Jan Paul Buschdorf first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Mutations in ATCAY that encodes the brain-specific protein BNIP-H (or Caytaxin) lead to Cayman cerebellar ataxia. The summary also notes a further point. BNIP-H binds to glutaminase, a neurotransmitter-producing enzyme, and affects its activity and intracellular localization. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002786:
Etienne Levavasseur led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was regulating factors of PrP res glycosylation in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease - implications for the dissemination and the diagnosis of human prion strains. Authorship is credited in the record to Etienne Levavasseur and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The glycoprofile of pathological prion protein (PrP res ) is widely used as a diagnosis marker in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and is thought to. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002886:
Leendert A. Trouw, Marcin Okroj, Koba Kupreishvili and co-authors examined heart attack tissue in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When blood flow drops, heart muscle cells die, and dying cells are known to bind blood proteins such as IgM and C-reactive protein. The team asked where a complement blocker called C4b-binding protein appears.

They found the protein present in harmed areas during the acute phase, the early stage after the attack. It also covered a larger area than the complement protein C3. The detail helps heart researchers picture how the immune cleanup after an attack is kept in check.
plos-pone-0002986:
Patrick Linsel-Nitschke, Anika Götz, Jeanette Erdmann and co-authors used a common LDL receptor variant to test lifelong cholesterol effects in 2008. Rare faults in the LDLR gene cause familial high cholesterol and raise coronary disease risk. What milder common variation does over a lifetime was less known.

Their Mendelian randomisation design treats inherited variants as a natural lifelong trial. The title reports that lifelong lower LDL cholesterol from this variant decreases coronary artery disease risk. Published in PLOS ONE, the logic strengthens the case that early, lasting cholesterol lowering protects the heart. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003086:
Ben MacArthur, Colin Please and Richard Oreffo modeled randomness in induced pluripotency in 2008. Making induced pluripotent stem cells from adult cells by adding key transcription factors holds significant medical promise. Current techniques then relied on viral infection and so were not viable for therapy at the time.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors examine stochasticity, the random element, in the molecular mechanisms of reprogramming. Randomness explains why only a few treated cells convert and why timing varies so much. Models of that chance can guide safer, more efficient protocols. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003186:
James J. McDevitt, Donald K. Milton, Stephen N. Rudnick and colleagues test ultraviolet light against poxviruses in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In a smallpox outbreak caused by bioterrorism, delays in vaccination could lead to significant secondary spread. In the early phase, spread would occur especially where infected persons gather, such as hospital rooms.

The team test whether upper-room UVC light inactivates poxviruses in a simulated hospital room. Readers get evidence on an air-cleaning measure that can run while people are present. Such passive controls matter for infection safety beyond any single outbreak scenario.
plos-pone-0003286:
Christine Braquart-Varnier, Marion Lachat, Juline Herbinière and colleagues study a common symbiont's effect on host immunity in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. After decades during which endosymbionts were considered silent in their hosts, in particular concerning the immune system, recent studies revealed the contrary. The team address the effect of Wolbachia, the most prevalent endosymbiont in arthropods, on host defences.

The title reports that Wolbachia mediate variation of host immunocompetence. Readers see a resident bacterium shaping how well its host fights other infections. That influence matters because Wolbachia is used to control insect-borne disease.
plos-pone-0003386:
Xiao-Bing Zhang and co-authors looked at how menthol acts in the brain in this 2008 paper. Menthol is the cooling compound from mint leaves, used in food and medicine. In outer nerves, it works by opening a cold sensor called TRPM8. Brain effects hinted that menthol had a second target as well.

The team found that menthol also acts on A-type GABA receptors in the brain. These receptors are the main calming switches of the central nervous system. Acting on both targets may explain menthol's wide range of effects. The finding adds a brain target to a very familiar compound.
plos-pone-0003486:
Becca Asquith weighed the costs and gains of HIV escape in this 2008 paper. Killer T cells hunt HIV inside infected cells. The virus can mutate to dodge that surveillance. Dodging may weaken immune control, at least for a while.

Asquith calculated the selective advantage of those escape variants. She also weighed their part in HLA-linked risk of faster AIDS. HLA genes shape which viral pieces T cells can see. The math clarifies how much escape really buys the virus over years. Escape also shapes which viral forms spread from one person to the next.
plos-pone-0003586:
Smanla Tundup and co-authors tested a tuberculosis protein pair in this 2008 paper. Many PE and PPE proteins of the TB germ sit on its surface or are secreted. They are thought to vary to dodge host immunity. Their exact roles remain elusive.

The pair PE25 and PPE41 are produced from one shared operon. Together they elicited stronger humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. Earlier work showed PPE41 alone raised high B cell responses. A matched pair may serve vaccine design against an evasive pathogen. TB still kills over a million people a year, mostly in poor countries.
plos-pone-0003686:
Katarina Fredriksson, Inga Tjäder, Pernille Keller, and colleagues published this intensive care study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Patients with sepsis in intensive care often develop failure of several organs. Their skeletal muscle stays weak long after, which slows recovery. The team had already shown muscle energy enzymes are impaired in these patients.

They found the dynamics of mitochondria in muscle were out of order, too. The muscle's set of active genes shifted along with the failure. The work traces the deep weakness of severe sepsis down to disturbed energy machinery inside muscle cells.
plos-pone-0003786:
Peyman Khorsand and Frances Chance published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A neuron's total input has two parts that can change on their own: its average level and its variance. Those two parts may act as separate information channels. The authors examined what happens when they shift fast.

They used spiking models to track the brief responses of neurons to rapid changes in mean and variance. The firing dynamics differed for the two kinds of change. The work shows how single cells read two streams of information carried by the same incoming signals.
plos-pone-0003886:
Jana C. Vamosi and Steven M. Vamosi wrote on extinction risk in the tropics in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article opens with a known pattern: species grow more numerous toward the equator. That rich tropical life now faces heavy losses, often called a biodiversity crisis. Such losses could wear away the pattern itself over time.

The authors argue that extinction risk climbs, not falls, in the tropics. They weigh why tropical species may be less able to absorb added pressure. Their case warns that the richest regions need the strongest protection. It reframes conservation planning around where risk and richness meet.
plos-pone-0003986:
Tanvi S. Sharma, Jane Hughes, Amarylis Murillo, and co-authors sought better markers for HIV in children in 2008. Treatment choices for infected children rest on viral load and CD4 counts. Those measures have limits, and backup markers are needed. The team focused on CD8 T cells and one receptor.

Their PLOS ONE article measures the interleukin-7 receptor alpha on CD8 cells. Levels of that receptor may reflect disease status in children. A blood marker that tracks status could sharpen treatment timing. The study adds a candidate to the short list of such markers. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004086:
Adrian G. Dyer and Quoc C. Vuong asked how insect brains recognize turned objects in 2008. Recognizing a 3D object from a new angle is hard for visual systems. Full 3D reconstruction demands heavy computation. Small insect brains manage it with limited resources.

Their PLOS ONE article reports insects use image interpolation mechanisms. The brain fills between stored views rather than rebuilding the object. That shortcut needs far less computation than model-based recognition. It offers design ideas for machine vision with tiny processors. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004186:
Lotte Wieten and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heat shock proteins can calm inflammation, an effect shown in animal models of inflammatory disease and in patients. How that calming effect works was poorly understood.

The team studied how a mycobacterial heat shock protein, HSP70, suppresses proteoglycan-induced arthritis, a joint inflammation model. They report that IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine, is required for the suppression. Naming IL-10 as a required middleman helps explain how a stress protein can quiet an inflamed joint. That names a middleman other treatments might aim at.
plos-pone-0004286:
Johannes Hirrlinger and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cre and LoxP recombination is the gold standard for switching genes in mice, but promoters driving Cre are often active in many cell types. That makes it hard to target a narrow subset of cells.

The authors present split-Cre complementation, in which Cre is divided into halves that work only when brought together. Coincident activity of two different genes in the same cell can then switch the system on. The trick sharpens genetic targeting to cells defined by two traits at once.
plos-pone-0004386:
Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis, shortened to MAP, infects many animal hosts. It has long been studied in cattle disease. Valentina Rosu, Niyaz Ahmed, Daniela Paccagnini, and co-authors tested its link to diabetes. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used targeted immune tests, called immunoassays. They compared people with type-1 and type-2 diabetes.

The authors report their tests confirm a link with type-1 diabetes. The same tests did not show that link for type-2 diabetes. Type-1 diabetes involves the immune system attacking insulin-making cells. A germ that interacts with immunity is therefore of real interest. The paper adds weight to one lead on what may help trigger the disease.
plos-pone-0004486:
Gene chip results can wobble for technical reasons that have nothing to do with biology, warn Cinda Scott, Jeff VanWye, M Danielle McDonald, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene expression varies a lot between individuals and populations, and measuring it well matters. Technical variation creeps in from RNA handling, the day of the run, and other lab steps.

The team carried out a technical analysis of cDNA microarrays, measuring how large these non-biological effects are. Knowing the size of the wobble tells researchers how many samples they need before a real difference can be trusted. It also shows which lab steps deserve the most care. Studies that skip this groundwork risk reporting lab noise as if it were a discovery about life.
plos-pone-0004586:
Two chemical marks on one protein may work as a binary switch, report Sudharsana Ande, Saby Moulik, and Suresh Mishra in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is prohibitin, an evolutionarily conserved, multifunctional protein found in many cell compartments, including the cell membrane. The mechanisms behind its many functions are not fully explored.

The team reports, for the first time on their account, an interaction between two modifications of prohibitin: one called O-GlcNAc modification, a sugar tag, and tyrosine phosphorylation, a phosphate tag. If the two marks influence each other, they can act like a switch with two states. Switches of this kind let one protein give different orders in different cell states, a neat economy for the cell.
plos-pone-0004686:
Maria Lodeiro and colleagues mapped how the hunger hormone ghrelin switches on a growth signal, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Ghrelin is best known for driving hunger, but it also acts on many cell pathways. One key path runs through a protein called Akt, which helps cells grow and stay alive.

The team used human kidney cells fitted with the ghrelin sensor. They traced which helper proteins link ghrelin to Akt, with and without one key scaffold. Step by step maps like this show how one hormone can have wide effects. They also point to spots where drugs might tune the signal.
plos-pone-0004786:
Christian Agrillo and colleagues tested use of number by fish, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Work on infants, mammals, birds, and fish shows basic number sense predates human language. Debate persists, though, on whether animals truly represent numbers or judge by non numerical cues like size, density, or total area of the items shown.

The team designed tests to separate true number use from such cues. Fish still used number when other cues were controlled. The result supports an ancient, shared number sense. It suggests counting roots run deep in vertebrate evolution. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004886:
Colin Lickwar and colleagues showed the Set2 Rpd3S pathway suppresses cryptic copying regardless of gene length or frequency, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In cells lacking histone methyltransferase Set2, initiation of RNA polymerase II occurs inappropriately within protein coding regions rather than proximal promoters. Prior reports claimed cryptic copying depended on gene length or copying frequency, prompting systematic tests across gene classes in yeast lacking pathway components.

Suppression proves universal across tested genes. Chromatin safeguards fidelity everywhere genes are read. Cryptic transcripts could produce harmful proteins. Quality control is genome wide. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004986:
Sirtuins are proteins linked to lifespan and metabolism. Mammals have seven of them. Three work inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Helen Cooper and colleagues studied one of those, SIRT3, in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined the mouse Sirt3 gene. They found a new splice variant of it.

The variant encodes the mitochondrial precursor protein. That is the form that gets imported into mitochondria. The discovery reveals a fresh route for producing SIRT3. Splicing choices decide which form the cell makes. The finding adds a piece to the longevity-protein puzzle. It also warns that one gene can hide several distinct products.
plos-pone-0005086:
Cells may communicate with light, not just chemicals. A few studies report that cells emit photons as signals. Daniel Fels tested that idea directly in PLOS ONE in 2009. He placed cells where a glass barrier separated them. The glass blocks molecules from passing. It lets light through.

Cells on one side influenced cells on the other side. The influence persisted across the barrier. Chemical contact cannot explain it. Light is the remaining carrier. The result suggests photons carry messages between cells. That claim is bold and needs replication. The study gives it a careful, simple test that others can repeat.
plos-pone-0005186:
Atrazine is a weed killer used widely on farms in the United States. Maps of heavy atrazine use overlap in striking ways with maps of high obesity rates. Lim and colleagues tested in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether long exposure to the chemical harms cell energy and insulin response.

As the title states, chronic exposure caused mitochondrial dysfunction and insulin resistance in their tests. Mitochondria are the cell parts that make energy, so damage there can shift whole-body metabolism. The work raises a pointed question about farm chemicals and diabetes risk, and it gives other labs a clear claim to test.
plos-pone-0005286:
The bread mold Neurospora crassa has a sequenced genome, but many of its predicted genes still lack known functions. Kasuga and colleagues took an evolutionary approach to that annotation gap in PLOS ONE in 2009, one that does not depend on lab tests of each gene.

The team related how widely each gene is shared across species to features of the genome itself. Old, widely shared genes behave differently from young, narrow ones. Using ancestry as a guide can suggest gene roles at genome scale and prioritize which genes deserve costly lab study.
plos-pone-0005386:
Whether cold changes cell membranes, and how, has been poorly characterized. Chen and colleagues used advanced imaging to watch lipid raft markers on T cells under cold in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rafts are small, ordered patches in the membrane that gather signaling proteins.

Cold caused micro-scale and nano-scale reorganization of raft markers, including GM1 and CD59. The markers gathered at mounds where the T cell membrane fluctuates. Temperature, it turns out, remodels the membrane's layout, which could change how immune cells signal in the cold. T cells must work in fever and in cold limbs alike. So a membrane that re-sorts itself with heat or cold could shift how well a shot or a drug works on a cold day.
plos-pone-0005486:
Ramaswamy Krishnan and colleagues studied how cells answer stretching in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Cells grip their surroundings and pull on them, and tissues such as the heart and lungs stretch them again and again. When stretched, the cell's inner frame can either stiffen or soften.

The team measured which answer cells give and what controls the choice. A stiffening answer protects the cell, while softening lets it flow and heal. Knowing the switch matters for understanding blood vessels, lungs, and wounds, where cells live under constant push and pull. The balance between the two answers also affects how tissues recover after strain or injury.
plos-pone-0005586:
Hong Lee and co-authors tested engineered stem cells in a mouse stroke model for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Human neural stem cells placed in a mouse brain after bleeding stroke had earlier helped the animals recover. Too few of the placed cells survived, though, which limited the gain.

The team altered the cells to make extra Akt1, a protein that promotes survival. The altered cells lived better, protected nerve tissue, and improved how the mice moved and behaved. Boosting survival is a key step toward cell therapy for stroke. Stroke leaves many people disabled, and cell repair remains one of the few hopes for gains after the event.
plos-pone-0005686:
Zhihua Zhang and Jianzhi Zhang explored a puzzle about networks in 2009: small worlds that hold big worlds inside them. Many real networks, from brains to food webs, are called small-world because any two points link through few steps. Yet random networks share that trait, so it says less than it seems.

The pair looked closer at how those short paths are built in real versus random networks. Inside the small-world pattern they found a richer, larger structure. Their point is that a single number, the average path length, hides what makes real networks special. The work pushes network science toward measures that capture real design.
plos-pone-0005786:
Juha Laurila and co-authors showed in 2009 that an antioxidant enzyme can slow the rush of immune cells into injured tissue. After blood flow is cut and restored, immune cells pour in, helping repair yet also causing harm. The enzyme SOD3, which works outside cells, tempers that flow.

The enzyme cut migration by adjusting adhesion molecules and cytokine signals, the hooks and calls that guide cells. Tuning the inflow, rather than blocking it, fits the dual nature of inflammation. The results suggest SOD3-based ideas for stroke and heart injury care, where this cell rush does real damage.
plos-pone-0005886:
Nicole Piazza and co-authors put fruit flies on an exercise program in 2009 and measured the payoff in old age. Loss of mobility is a top reason older people enter care, and falls add injury and cost. Exercise helps, but the biology of its benefit is easier to dissect in flies.

Trained young flies kept better mobility and heart performance as they aged than untrained ones. The result supports early, regular activity as a buffer against decline. Flies let the team separate exercise from diet and other human confounders. The model now invites gene hunts for the pathways exercise engages.
plos-pone-0005986:
Dentists now try to heal early tooth decay rather than drill it out. Reina Tanaka, Yo Shibata, Atsufumi Manabe and colleagues explored one healing aid in 2009: polarized dental enamel. Their PLOS ONE paper asks how well treated enamel can take minerals back in, since rebuilding mineral is the key to halting a young cavity.

One snag is that minerals tend to rebuild only the outer skin of the tooth, sealing the deeper part off. A charged enamel surface might draw minerals deeper. The study tests that potential in the lab. Work of this kind backs the shift toward gentle, drill-free care for teeth caught at the first stage of decay.
plos-pone-0006086:
Marks laid on the proteins that spool DNA can be passed to daughter cells. Matthew VerMilyea, Laura O'Neill and Bryan Turner tested that passing in the earliest mouse embryo in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies induced histone modifications in the preimplantation embryo, a stage with very few cells, which had long blocked this kind of test.

The marks were inherited without the genes being read, a transcription-independent heritability. A mark that copies itself through cell divisions gives the embryo a memory beyond its DNA letters. The result bears on how early development is guided, and on the wider question of what, besides DNA, a parent cell hands down.
plos-pone-0006186:
A female mammal is born with a pool of resting egg follicles that must last her whole life. Krishna Jagarlamudi and colleagues removed the gene Pten only from mouse egg cells, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Pten normally restrains a growth signal called PI3K, and earlier work showed that lifting the brake wakes follicles too early.

The deletion revealed that the signal's job changes with the stage of the egg's growth. Timing matters: the same pathway can help at one stage and harm at another. Waking too many follicles early can drain the pool and shorten fertility. The findings guide research on ovarian ageing and fertility care.
plos-pone-0006286:
Turning embryonic stem cells into neurons in a dish could one day repair injured nerves. Elsa Abranches and colleagues map that conversion in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Making neurons from stem cells is a promising route to cells for neural tissue repair and replacement therapies.

The authors lay out a road map comparing lab differentiation with neurogenesis in the embryo. Knowing the true sequence helps labs steer cells to the right stage. Immature or mixed cells would be unsafe for therapy. A careful map is groundwork for future nervous system treatments.
plos-pone-0006386:
Crohn's disease is a long term gut illness with no known single cause. Janet Jansson and her team used broad chemical scans of gut samples in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Genes, the home setting, and the germs of the gut all play a part in the disease.

The scans found chemical signs made by gut germs that mark the disease state. Such signs could one day help doctors spot Crohn's with a simple test. They also hint at which gut germs help drive the illness. That gives drug and diet work a clearer place to start.
plos-pone-0006486:
Francesca Boscia and co-authors tested a growth factor's effects in the injured hippocampus for PLOS ONE in 2009. GDNF, short for glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, is a potent survival factor for several neuron types. That includes neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub. The team exposed hippocampal regions CA1 and CA3 to injury conditions.

Their title reports that GDNF selectively activates microglia, the brain's immune cells, and promotes neuronal survival there. Selective action matters, since broad effects can harm as well as help. The finding supports GDNF as a candidate protectant after brain injury. It also clarifies which cells mediate that protection.
plos-pone-0006586:
Noa Regev and co-authors studied a protein pair that tunes nerve cell channels in PLOS ONE in 2009. A channel pair called KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 forms the M-channel in nerve cells. M-channels keep nerve firing in check. Other proteins can tune these channels, and each channel type is tuned in its own way. The team tested how syntaxin 1A, a protein best known for helping cells release signals, interacts with KCNQ2.

Their title stresses that this interaction is selective: syntaxin picks KCNQ2 over close kin. A picky link like this hints at fine control of firing before a signal is sent. Such control matters in epilepsy, where faults in these channels are known to play a role.
plos-pone-0006686:
Irma Casas and co-authors evaluated tuberculosis blood tests in health care workers for PLOS ONE in 2009. Hospital staff face a raised risk of latent tuberculosis infection. Latent infection means the bacteria are present without active illness. Finding it early matters for staff and patients alike. The older tuberculin skin test has known limits.

The team compared two interferon-gamma release assays against the skin test. The assays were the QuantiFERON-TB Gold In Tube and T-SPOT.TB tests. They measured immune responses in workers with recent infection risk. Comparing the three methods shows where the blood tests agree or differ. The results help hospitals choose screening methods for their staff.
plos-pone-0006786:
Sandra Chanraud and co-authors studied memory in people who had stopped drinking in PLOS ONE in 2009. Detoxified alcoholics often show episodic memory deficits. Episodic memory is recall of personal events. Reports disagreed about which brain regions stay intact in these patients. The authors combined memory testing with brain microstructure imaging.

They related memory scores to grey matter microstructure changes. Altered microstructure contributed to the memory deficits observed. The link helps explain why memory suffers even without obvious brain shrinkage. It also suggests targets for rehabilitation after detoxification. Measuring microstructure may track recovery of memory over time.
plos-pone-0006886:
David M. Vickers, Qian Zhang, and Nathaniel D. Osgood modeled repeated chlamydia infection inside a single host in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chlamydia trachomatis is a common human pathogen. It can cause serious harm to reproductive health. The body's aggressive inflammatory response cuts both ways. It builds a person's immunity, yet the same response can damage tissue and leave lasting harm. Repeat infections are a normal part of this disease's course.

The team built two mathematical models of how the bacteria grow within a host. They used the models to compare the immune outcomes of one infection with the outcomes of repeated infections. The work shows how each new infection can reshape both defense and damage. That helps explain why a common infection can stay mild in one case and cause lasting reproductive harm in another.
plos-pone-0006986:
Jose Martin-Subero, Ole Ammerpohl, Marina Bibikova, and colleagues charted DNA methylation in blood cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Leukemias and lymphomas are marked by disturbed methylation patterns. Past studies usually covered few genes or few disease types. A broad survey across many blood cancers was still missing.

The team used microarrays to profile hundreds of these neoplasms. In total, they studied three hundred sixty-seven cases. The shared and distinct marks they found help sort these cancers. Methylation profiles may also point to genes that treatment could switch back on.
plos-pone-0007086:
Daniel Cohen, Roberto Morfino, and Michel Maharbiz turned a home printer into a lab tool in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their goal was cheap, precise control of gene expression in space and time. They modified a consumer inkjet printer for chemical dosing. The printer delivered diffusible regulator chemicals onto a gel culture of E. coli.

Patterns of chemicals switched bacterial genes on in matching patterns. The system kept two-dimensional control running over time. A printer-based rig costs far less than standard microfluidics. It puts pattern experiments within reach of teaching labs and small teams.
plos-pone-0007186:
Kwanjune J. Seung, David B. Omatayo, Salmaan Keshavjee, and colleagues reported early treatment results for drug-resistant tuberculosis in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers Lesotho in southern Africa. The country has a high rate of HIV infection, which makes tuberculosis harder to treat.

Little was known about treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in such settings at the time. The authors review the first cohort registered in the Lesotho national program, which began in July of that period. They report early outcomes, giving program planners and clinicians evidence from a difficult real-world treatment setting.
plos-pone-0007286:
Jan-Rung Mo, Anjili Mathur, Minilik Angagaw, and colleagues studied spleen removal in a blood disease model in PLOS ONE in 2009. An enlarged spleen develops in many diseases, but its specific role is rarely proven. In polycythemia vera, a JAK2 mutation drives spleen growth and raises hematocrit, the share of red cells in blood.

The authors test splenectomy, surgical spleen removal, in mice with this condition. They report that splenectomy normalizes hematocrit. Their result gives the spleen a direct pathogenic role in this model. That role could inform treatment choices for patients with enlarged spleens.
plos-pone-0007386:
David Meinke, Colleen Sweeney, and Rosanna Muralla integrated two maps of the Arabidopsis genome in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The classical genetic map of this model plant includes many embryo-defective genes. Mutations in those essential genes kill embryos, and many remained uncloned despite their importance for understanding seed development.

Hundreds more essential genes had been cloned but not mapped. The authors connect the genetic and physical maps. They identify mapped alleles of cloned essential genes. Their integration helps researchers match old mutant names to modern gene sequences, speeding seed biology work.
plos-pone-0007486:
Deheng Wang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a brain receptor part called NR2B and its role in learning. NR2B belongs to the NMDA receptor, which detects coincident signals between neurons. One major theory calls NR2B a universal rate-limiting factor for learning across species. The team tested that idea in rats engineered to carry extra NR2B.

The transgenic rats showed enhanced memory. They also showed stronger long-term potentiation, the lasting strengthening of connections between neurons. Yet long-term depression, a form of connection weakening in the same region, stayed normal. So extra NR2B boosts some forms of plasticity without breaking others. That selectivity supports NR2B as a genuine dial for memory. It also hints at safer ways to enhance cognition than blanket stimulation.
plos-pone-0007586:
Stefano Iacovelli and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how T cells grow up in the thymus. Thymus development and T cell maturation proceed together, guided by constant crosstalk between young thymocytes and the tissue around them. A maturation block at any stage can cripple immunity. The team studied a protein called EVA1, expressed in lymphoid tissue, and its role in early T cell stages.

EVA1 expression proved required for thymocytes to pass from the DN1 stage through to DN3. Without it, developing immune cells stall at that early gate. Each stage of T cell birth is a checkpoint with its own gatekeepers. EVA1 now joins that list for a key early transition. The result adds a player to the choreography by which the immune system builds its frontline cells.
plos-pone-0007686:
Beatriz Navarro and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns grapevine plants infected with viroids. Viroids are tiny circles of RNA that code for no proteins at all. They still copy themselves inside plant cells and move through the plant.

Using deep sequencing, the team read the small RNAs that infected vines produce from the viroid. Plants cut invading RNA into small pieces as a defense, a process called RNA silencing. The pattern of those pieces gives new clues about how the defense works and how viroids manage to survive it.
plos-pone-0007786:
Kei-ichi Katayama and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines the inner ears of mice lacking a gene called Slitrk6. The Slitrk proteins sit in cell membranes and share features with guidance molecules. They help wire the nervous system during development.

Without Slitrk6, the inner ear's wiring grew disorganized. Neurons that carry sound signals were also lost. Hearing depends on exact connections between ear and brain. The mouse findings show one gene that keeps those connections orderly. Such genes are candidates when doctors hunt for causes of inherited hearing loss.
plos-pone-0007886:
Yeh-Chuin Poh and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It watches cells respond to physical force in real time. Mechanical forces shape the function of every tissue and organ. How force becomes chemical activity inside a cell was unclear.

The team applied force to living cells and tracked a switch protein, Rac GTPase. Rac switched on rapidly after force was applied. The activation did not depend on Src, a well-known signaling enzyme. That independence redraws the wiring diagram of force sensing. Understanding mechanotransduction matters for fields from wound healing to heart disease.
plos-pone-0007986:
Karen May and colleagues asked how malaria matter crosses from mother to unborn child in PLOS ONE in 2009. The placenta is the gate between the two bloodstreams. The team used a lab model in which a human placenta is kept alive and fed fluid outside the body.

Malaria antigens, pieces of the parasite, crossed the gate when the mother's antibodies carried them. That antibody help shapes what the fetus meets and learns before birth. The result may explain why a mother's past malaria can change her child's risk in the first years of life.
plos-pone-0008086:
Linqi Zhou and colleagues asked why deleting one yeast gene can harm many traits at once in PLOS ONE in 2009. That spread of effects is called pleiotropy. Genes whose loss hurts growth in many settings share certain traits, and the team hunted for what those traits are.

Two stood out: genes run by chromatin control, and genes that sit at busy crossroads in cell networks. A crossroads gene, once lost, sends ripples far and wide. The rule helps predict which gene losses will ripple and which will stay local, a guide for both yeast work and drug side effects.
plos-pone-0008186:
Gillian McGovern, Neil Mabbott, and Martin Jeffrey studied scrapie in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Scrapie belongs to the prion diseases, infectious brain disorders of humans and animals. In these diseases, an abnormal prion protein builds up in the brain and lymph tissue. Before reaching the brain, the infection passes through that lymph tissue.

The authors focused on follicular dendritic cells, which trap immune complexes there. They asked how scrapie affects the maturation cycle of these cells. Changes in trapping could shape how the disease spreads toward the brain. The findings add detail to the early stages of prion infection.
plos-pone-0008286:
Mark van der Linden and colleagues characterized pneumococcal bacteria from animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Streptococcus pneumoniae is best known as a human pathogen. Between 1986 and 2008, it was also isolated from many animals. The collection included guinea pigs, cats, horses, dogs, dolphins, rats, and a gorilla. Samples came from veterinary laboratories, zoos, and laboratory animals.

The team used molecular methods to type these isolates. Comparing animal strains with human ones shows how widely the bacterium travels. It also reveals which types infect which hosts. Such data matter for animal health and for tracking disease.
plos-pone-0008386:
Yoko Kawaguchi-Ito and colleagues traced a plant virus-like agent over fifteen years in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hop stunt first emerged as a mystery disorder in Japanese commercial hops in the 1940s. Its cause is a viroid, a tiny infectious RNA. Isolates came from hop, grapevine, plum, and citrus hosts. The team infected hops with isolates from each source.

Grapevines proved a symptomless reservoir for transmission to hop crops. A crop can thus spread disease while showing no signs. Fifteen years of evolutionary analysis traced how the viroid changed. The work guides protection of hop farming.
plos-pone-0008486:
Robert Haney and co-authors compare transposable elements in fruit flies in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Transposable elements are DNA bits that can insert into new sites. Heat-shock genes switch on when cells face heat stress. Their promoter regions, which control gene activity, hold many P element insertions. That pattern stands out in natural populations of Drosophila melanogaster. The team screen those sequences in detail.

They contrast insertions in heat-shock promoters with control regions. The contrast tests if the clustering is random or favored. A favored pattern would hint that insertions help flies adapt to heat. The work bears on how mobile DNA shapes gene control.
plos-pone-0008586:
Andrei Okorokov and co-authors solve a DNA repair filament structure in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Meiotic recombination is a major source of genetic diversity. Its defects in humans lead to syndromes such as Down and Klinefelter syndromes. Human Dmc1 is a recombinase crucial for faithful recombination. It is a homologue of RecA and Rad51, classic recombination proteins. The team determine the structure of hDmc1 bound to single-stranded DNA. The complex forms a helical filament.

Their structure reveals the principles of that filament's architecture. It shows how Dmc1 grips DNA to search for matching sequences. Faithful matching prevents the errors behind chromosomal syndromes. Structural insight may guide understanding of infertility linked to recombination faults.
plos-pone-0008686:
Heike Lux, Heiko Flammann, Mathias Hafner, and coworkers took a close look at a curious human gene. PEG10 sits on chromosome 7 and came from an ancient virus-like element. Fathers pass on the active copy. The gene makes at least two proteins through a shifting trick during protein building.

Their 2010 PLOS ONE study mapped how PEG10 is organized, read, and turned into protein. Extra PEG10 activity shows up in some cancers, so its normal control matters. The team checked where its messages start and how the shifting trick works. A clearer map of this gene aids work on growth, the placenta, and tumors.
plos-pone-0008786:
Kornelia Edes, Pamela Cassidy, Paul Shami, and colleagues paired a gas-releasing drug with a weakened defense enzyme. Their colon cancer study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. JS-K is a prodrug that releases nitric oxide inside cells. That gas can push cancer cells to die. An enzyme called thioredoxin reductase 1 helps tumor cells survive oxidative stress. It also blunts many drug attacks.

When the enzyme was knocked down, JS-K killed colon cancer cells far better. The pairing turned a modest drug into a strong one. Combination strategies like this aim to beat tumor defenses. The work suggests testing both moves together in further models.
plos-pone-0008886:
David Naeger, Jeffrey Martin, Elizabeth Sinclair, and colleagues counted virus-specific T cells in people on long HIV treatment. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cytomegalovirus, or CMV, infects most adults and stays for life. In healthy people, huge shares of T cells stand guard against it. Such large standing armies are linked to faster immune aging. HIV treatment changes that balance in unknown ways.

Even after years of antiretroviral therapy, CMV-specific T cells stayed very high. Treatment did not shrink the CMV guard force. A persistent CMV burden may keep driving immune aging in treated HIV. That possibility argues for adding CMV control to HIV care.
plos-pone-0008986:
Martina Nilsson and co-authors put the supposed bones of a medieval saint on the lab bench, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Saint Birgitta of Sweden, who lived from 1303 to 1373, is one of Europe's patron saints. Legend says her skull rests in a shrine at Vadstena Abbey in Sweden. A second skull there is said to be her daughter Katarina's.

The team analysed the remains with modern dating and DNA-era methods. Testing old relics can confirm or unsettle centuries of tradition. Their results addressed whether the skulls fit the women's ages and era. The study shows how science can check history without dismissing it.
plos-pone-0009086:
Ikechi Okpechi and co-authors tested the obesity hormone's gene against kidney disease signs in South Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chronic kidney disease is a growing global health problem. Obesity raises the risk of developing it. Leptin, the hormone that reports body fat, tracks with fat mass.

The study population was Xhosa, a South African group rarely included in genetics work. Variants at chosen spots in the leptin gene were tested. The team compared them with markers of kidney trouble. Any link would tie fat signalling to kidney risk in this population.
plos-pone-0009186:
Sungsam Gong and Tom Blundell published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It asks why some positions in human proteins almost never change. Each person's proteins carry small differences, often a single amino acid swapped for another. Some swaps are harmless, while others break the protein and cause disease.

The authors catalogued features of protein structure and function that limit where such swaps can occur. A buried position, or one that holds the protein's shape, tolerates far less change. Their catalogue reflects both helpful and neutral change left by human evolution. It helps readers judge which newly found variants are likely to matter for health.
plos-pone-0009286:
Chihiro Kawaguchi and co-authors published this mouse clock study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eyes do more than see images; light also sets the body clock. A pigment called melanopsin drives that nonvisual sensing. It resets the daily clock, shapes sleep and activity, and controls the pupil's response to light.

The team studied mice lacking PACAP, a signaling peptide in the same system. The mutant mice showed abnormal responses that depended on light conditions. Their daily activity also started at odd times. The results show PACAP helps the clock read light correctly, fine-tuning how animals match their rhythm to the day.
plos-pone-0009386:
Barkha Patel and co-authors published this mouse study of ALS in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eating less, called caloric restriction, extends life in many animals. It usually works by cutting oxidative stress and delaying disease. The G93A mouse models amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the disease that kills motor neurons.

In these mice, the usual rules reversed. Caloric restriction shortened life rather than extending it. The team traced the harm to more lipid peroxidation, more inflammation, and more cell death in the mice. The warning is clear: a therapy that helps healthy animals can hurt when a specific disease is present.
plos-pone-0009486:
Eva Greganova, Manfred Heller, and Peter Butikofer studied a parasite protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness in Africa. One of its key proteins carries a rare chemical tag called EPG. In mammals and plants, the tag is fixed to two set spots on the protein. In the parasite, the pattern differs.

The team found the part of the protein that bears and mediates the tag in the parasite. That part works in its own way, unlike the host version. A trait found only in the parasite is valuable to drug hunters. Blocking it could harm the germ while sparing the person it infects.
plos-pone-0009586:
Jean-Bernard Caron, Simon Conway Morris, and Degan Shu described ancient fossils in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fossils come from Cambrian rocks in Canada and China. Each bears a ring of tentacles around the mouth. Genes and body plans unite sea stars and acorn worms as one group. The early history of that group, and of our own wider kin, is almost unknown.

The authors read these tentacled animals as primitive deuterostomes. Deuterostomes are the great branch that includes backboned animals like us. That reading gives a face to ancestors once only guessed at. It pushes the known record of our deep lineage back to over five hundred million years ago.
plos-pone-0009686:
Animals with fast metabolisms burn energy quickly, and some scientists think that pace also speeds up mutation. Angela McGaughran and Barbara Holland put that idea to a direct test in PLOS ONE in 2010. They checked whether metabolic rate predicts how much DNA varies within a single species.

The idea matters because mutation feeds evolution with new variation. If body pace drove mutation, fast-living species would change genetically faster than slow ones. Their analysis weighed the evidence across species at the within-species level. The paper gives the long-debated claim a careful, data-based check.
plos-pone-0009886:
Artificial cells need skins, and DNA can act like a programmable glue to build them. Maik Hadorn and Peter Eggenberger Hotz showed DNA guiding the self-assembly of artificial vesicles. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The vesicles are far simpler than real cells.

A vesicle is a tiny bubble wrapped in a thin membrane. DNA-mediated assembly uses matching DNA strands to pull parts together in set ways. Self-assembly means the pieces organize themselves without hands-on building. Such bubbles could one day carry drugs or mimic living cells in the lab.
plos-pone-0009986:
A weakened virus used for study can regain its strength with a single tiny change. John Morrill and colleagues watched that happen with Rift Valley fever virus in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rift Valley fever strikes livestock and people in Africa.

The starting virus was attenuated, weakened on purpose for safer study. It carried a single nucleotide substitution in its M segment RNA. From it, virulent virus accumulated rapidly in the mice. The case is a warning about how thin the line is between weakened and dangerous.
plos-pone-0010186:
The authors were Rachael Hawtin, David Stockett, Jo Ann Byl, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study described a cancer drug candidate called voreloxin. It targets topoisomerase II, an enzyme vital for copying DNA and sorting chromosomes. Existing drugs on that target work, but tumors often resist them and side effects limit their use in patients.

Voreloxin is a quinolone derivative that slips into DNA and poisons the target enzyme. A new chemical family on a proven target may dodge some known resistance routes. The paper lays out how the drug acts, a step toward clinical testing.
plos-pone-0010386:
Archana Patel, Manju Mamtani, Michael Dibley and others reviewed zinc treatment for childhood diarrhea in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diarrhea still kills many young children in poorer countries. Zinc had been known for over a decade to help treat it. Yet questions remained about how much it helps, and in which cases. The authors gathered past trials into one systematic review.

A systematic review weighs all fair tests together rather than cherry-picking. Their summary weighed zinc for both short, acute attacks and long, persistent ones. Clear totals help health agencies decide whether to supply zinc widely. Cheap treatments with solid proof are gold in global health. This review aimed to settle zinc's value with the full evidence in view.
plos-pone-0010486:
SiDe Li and co-workers showed that a mitochondrial enzyme tempers the growth-stopping power of p53 in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein p53 orders stressed cells to pause, self-destruct, or age out. Those orders follow a gene program p53 controls in the nucleus. Some of p53's anti-growth work, though, happens outside the nucleus. The team studied an enzyme in mitochondria called SirT3 in that context.

SirT3 removed chemical tags and thereby regulated p53-driven growth arrest. An enzyme in the cell's power plant thus influences a nuclear guardian. That cross-talk matters in cancer, where p53 is often lost or blocked. It also matters in aging, where both players are active. The study widens p53's known network into the mitochondria.
plos-pone-0010586:
Andreas Götz and colleagues tracked how gut bacteria feed while living inside human cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genome maps show what these bacteria could do in theory. The team wanted to measure what they actually burn for energy during infection.

Working with colorectal cancer cells grown in the lab, they traced carbon through the bacteria's chemistry. The pathogens relied on a narrower set of fuels than their genomes suggested. They also swapped metabolites with their host cells. A clear record of real feeding habits gives drug researchers targets that matter during infection, not just in a test tube.
plos-pone-0010686:
Lorenzo Sabatelli modeled drug resistance in parasitic worms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drugs that kill worms lose power as resistant worms spread. Health programs hope vaccines could join or replace drugs, but the effect of vaccines on resistance was not clear.

His computer model let people and worms mix in uneven patterns, as they do in real villages. Vaccination slowed the spread of resistance under many settings. Uneven mixing changed the speed of that spread. Models like this cannot replace field trials, but they help planners choose drug and vaccine mixes before resistance makes the choice for them.
plos-pone-0010786:
Maria Laura Polo and colleagues tested drug pairs against hormone-resistant breast cancer in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many breast cancers first answer hormone therapy, then learn to resist it. The team used a mouse cancer that becomes hormone-independent, grown in three-dimensional cultures that mimic real tissue better than flat dishes.

Two pathway blockers, aimed at PI3K and at MEK, were tested on the resistant model. Responses showed which pathway the resistant cells leaned on. The 3D system preserved hormone-independent behavior lost in flat culture. Better test beds mean drug pairs reach human trials with more honest odds, sparing patients combinations that only work in plastic dishes.
plos-pone-0010886:
Delphine Goven, Anne Boutten, Véronique Leçon-Malas and co-authors published this lung study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is a sudden lung collapse, often in young smokers, and its causes are poorly understood. The team suspected oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen, in the lung's resident immune cells.

They compared lung tissue from smoking and nonsmoking patients with the condition and from controls. In smokers, lung macrophages showed more of a chemical damage marker and higher levels of three protective proteins that neutralize oxidants and store iron safely. A low-oxygen control factor appeared involved in driving the response. Goven and colleagues paint the collapsed lung as a site of oxygen stress and counterattack, which may help explain why smoking raises the risk of recurrence.
plos-pone-0010986:
Silke Klee, Elzbieta Brzuszkiewicz, Herbert Nattermann and co-authors published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A chimpanzee in Africa died with symptoms of anthrax. Yet the bacterium isolated from it broke the rules of the anthrax species. It could move. It also lacked the usual prophages and a signature broken gene. The team sequenced its complete genome to find out what it was.

The genome held a chromosome plus three plasmids, two of which matched the anthrax virulence plasmids carrying the toxin and capsule genes. The chromosome itself resembled harmless relatives in the Bacillus cereus group. Klee and colleagues describe a hybrid threat: an ordinary-looking bacterium armed with anthrax weapons. Their finding blurs species lines used in biodefense and argues for plasmid-based detection of dangerous strains.
plos-pone-0011086:
Rose, Mueller, Gerstl and colleagues evaluated a rapid test in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their study took place during a 2007 city outbreak of meningitis in Burkina Faso. The illness was caused by a meningitis germ of group A, and fast diagnosis was vital for care and control.

The team checked how well a simple dipstick test performed in real outbreak conditions. A stick test needs no full lab, so health workers can use it close to patients. Good results would support wider use where labs are scarce. Fast answers during an outbreak can save lives and guide vaccine and drug use.
plos-pone-0011186:
Stich, Manrubia and Lazaro modeled mutation rates in PLOS ONE in 2010. Copying errors fuel evolution, but too many errors can be harmful. The authors asked whether groups of replicators do better by raising or lowering their mutation rate as conditions change.

Their model treats a variable rate as an adaptive strategy in its own right. Turning the dial up can speed adaptation in new settings, while turning it down protects gains. That idea helps explain why some germs evolve fast under stress. It adds a layer to how scientists think about the pace of evolution itself.
plos-pone-0011286:
De Luca, Klimentidis, Casazza and colleagues studied energy control across species in PLOS ONE in 2010. A family of cell surface proteins, called syndecans, was examined for its role in how the whole body budgets energy. Evidence from flies to mammals suggested a shared, conserved function.

The family did regulate whole body energy metabolism in their analysis. A conserved regulator is a promising lead for obesity and diabetes research, since its role survived long evolution. Drugs aimed at it would build on a basic system, not a narrow one. The study also shows the value of comparing simple and complex animals for metabolic clues.
plos-pone-0011386:
Carlyle Rogers, Zhenhua Guo, and John Stiller explored in 2010 how small changes to one part of the cell's copying machine ripple across the whole cell. RNA polymerase II copies DNA into RNA, and a flexible tail on the machine helps steer copying and message handling. Mutations in that tail are known to change cell behavior in complex ways.

Combining gene activity data with network analysis, the team connected specific tail mutations to wide changes in cell traits. The approach shows which downstream genes move together when one tail feature is altered. That mapping helps explain how a single repeated region can shape growth, stress response, and other traits at once. For molecular biology, the study offers a model for linking a tiny structural change to system-wide effects.
plos-pone-0011486:
Liang Ran and co-authors documented in 2010 the shrinking genome of a bacterium that lives inside other organisms. The cyanobacterium they studied fixes nitrogen, turning air's nitrogen into food its host can use, and it is passed directly from parent to offspring inside the host. A safe life with food provided lets a genome shed genes it no longer needs.

Their analysis charts that genome erosion in detail, showing losses consistent with a settled, dependent life. What remains is close to the essentials for its nitrogen-fixing job. The withering code is evolution's deal made visible: security inside a host, paid for with independence. Studying such reduced genomes teaches biologists what a minimal working cell requires, and how partnerships between species can become so tight that one partner can no longer live alone.
plos-pone-0011586:
Sievert Rohwer and Luan-Keng Wang measured feather replacement in the moustached tree swift for PLOS ONE in 2010. This tropical bird feeds in flight and spends much of its life in the air. Feathers wear out far faster than the bird itself, so they must be replaced often, at a real cost in energy and flight skill.

The authors counted and timed how flight feathers are shed and regrown across the year. Their numbers show how the bird spreads that cost so it can keep flying while moulting. The study helps explain how aerial birds fit a risky but vital task into a life spent on the wing.
plos-pone-0011686:
Diane Bridge and co-authors studied stress defences in the freshwater polyp Hydra vulgaris, in PLOS ONE in 2010. FoxO proteins help cells in animals from worms to humans respond to stress, including damage from oxygen by-products. Hydra is a simple cnidarian famous for its hardiness and slow ageing, making it a good test of how ancient these defences are.

The team examined how FoxO works in Hydra's stress responses. Their findings connect this simple animal's resilience to the same control system used by far more complex animals. That deep continuity suggests stress management by FoxO is an old invention of animal life.
plos-pone-0011786:
Luca Goitre and co-authors studied a disease gene's housekeeping role inside cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. KRIT1 faults cause cerebral cavernous malformations, abnormally enlarged and leaky brain capillaries that predispose people to seizures, deficits and fatal bleeding. A comprehensive analysis of what KRIT1 does in cells was still needed.

The team showed KRIT1 regulates the balance of reactive oxygen species, the damaging by-products of oxygen use, inside cells. Losing that control leaves cells exposed to oxidative harm. The antioxidant housekeeping role connects one gene to vessel fragility through basic cell chemistry.
plos-pone-0011886:
Cao Chen and colleagues prepared in 2010 specialized antibodies to profile a protein in the spinal fluid of people with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. That fatal brain disease is already known to raise levels of tau protein in spinal fluid, a sign widely used in diagnosis. What remained unknown was which forms of tau appear, since tau comes in several versions built from different gene pieces.

The team's exon-specific antibodies, each aimed at one piece of the protein, revealed distinct tau profiles in patients' fluid. A fingerprint of forms could sharpen diagnosis beyond a simple high-or-low reading. For a disease that is hard to confirm while a patient lives, a clearer spinal fluid pattern has real value.
plos-pone-0011986:
Johannes Brettschneider and co-workers tested in 2010 a spinal fluid signal that might forecast the course of a first multiple sclerosis-like episode. The episode type is called clinically isolated syndrome, and only some patients go on to full multiple sclerosis. B lymphocytes are now thought to matter in the disease, so B cell signals in spinal fluid are promising candidates.

The team evaluated CXCL13, a chemical that attracts B cells, as a prognostic marker in these patients. A marker measured at the first episode could tell doctors who needs early, strong treatment and who can safely wait. That sorting is one of the most practical problems in MS care.
plos-pone-0012086:
Nobuyuki Kawamura and co-workers described in 2010 how mice missing a proton pump part develop eye damage. The vacuolar-type ATPase acidifies cell compartments and is involved in proper development of visual function. Its a3 subunit is coded by the Tcirg1 gene, whose mutations cause severe recessive osteopetrosis, a bone disease, in humans.

In Tcirg1 mutant mice, the team found optic nerve compression alongside retinal degeneration. The pairing suggests the eye damage rides on the bone disease: overgrown bone squeezes the nerve that carries vision. Findings in the mouse help explain visual loss in children with this rare disease and mark where monitoring should focus.
plos-pone-0012186:
Nicholas Charlton and Alasdair Houston asked what bumble bees are really trying to gain as they forage, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models of bee behavior need a currency, a single measure the bee is assumed to maximize. For bumble bees the usual choice was the net rate of energy gathered, while honey bee behavior fits better with efficiency, the gain divided by the cost.

Reworking several earlier studies, the authors tested which currency actually predicts bumble bee choices. Getting the currency right matters because models built on it forecast how bees will work a field of flowers. Those forecasts feed into farming, since crops depend on wild bees choosing to visit them.
plos-pone-0012286:
Kuanyu Li, Anamika Singh, Daniel Crooks, and co-authors identified the switches that control the frataxin gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Friedreich ataxia, an inherited nerve disease, arises when a repeated DNA stretch inside the frataxin gene turns its output down. Raising that output again is an obvious treatment idea, but nobody knew exactly which transcription factors run the gene's promoter.

The team showed two named factors, SRF and TFAP2, regulate frataxin's expression. Any drug meant to boost frataxin must work through the gene's real controls, so naming them is the enabling step. It also gives researchers readouts to screen candidate compounds quickly in cells.
plos-pone-0012386:
Justin Clifton, Edinson Lucumi, Michael Myers and colleagues used zebrafish to hunt for compounds that block fat uptake from food, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Drugs that cut dietary fat absorption can improve blood fat levels in people at risk of heart disease, and they can support or replace statins. A fast whole-animal screen was needed to find new candidates.

Young zebrafish fed glowing fat let the team watch absorption live and test many compounds quickly. Several new blockers turned up in the screen. Because zebrafish share much gut and fat biology with humans, hits from this screen give chemists fresh starting points for safer fat-blocking medicines.
plos-pone-0012486:
Yukio Akaneya, Kazuhiro Sohya, Akihiko Kitamura and colleagues watched new synapses form in the young hippocampus, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Synapse building is a basic step in wiring the brain, and in the hippocampus it starts with sticky contacts between nerve endings and target cells. A signal pair named ephrin-A5 and EphA5 was suspected to guide that stickiness.

The team showed the pair's interaction actively induces synapse formation during early development. A defined molecular handshake for synapse birth is valuable knowledge. It feeds research on learning, memory, and conditions like autism where synapse numbers go wrong in early life.
plos-pone-0012586:
Frederikke Malinovsky, Peter Brodersen, Berthe Fiil and colleagues characterized a plant protein tied to controlled cell death, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Programmed cell death is a normal part of life in multicellular organisms. In plants, one form is the hypersensitive response, a scorched-earth defense that kills cells around an infection site to wall off pathogens.

The protein Lazarus1, a member of the DUF300 family, contributes to that death program and to death seen in the mutant acd11. Naming the executioners of plant cell death helps breeders and biotechnologists tune crop immunity, since a defense that kills too much tissue can cost as much yield as disease.
plos-pone-0012686:
Berniker, Voss and Kording modelled how the brain mixes fresh senses with past learning. People blend what they see and hear now with expectations built over a lifetime. Their 2010 paper studies priors, the brain's stored guesses, and how a learner should set them.

They show how good priors can be learned rather than fixed in advance. Getting this right matters for theories of perception and for building machines that learn like brains. The work links lab findings on human judgement to a clean learning rule. The model also predicts when strong priors help and when they mislead.
plos-pone-0012786:
Murdoch, Clawson, Yue and co-authors linked a pattern in the cow prion gene to mad cow disease rates. Classical BSE, the cattle prion disease behind mad cow outbreaks, can pass to people through food. The bovine prion gene, PRNP, has stretches where variants travel together and other stretches where they mix freely.

Their 2010 study of European Holstein cattle tied one such pattern to how often BSE appeared. A gene pattern tied to risk could help breeding and surveillance programmes. It also sharpens the science of prion diseases across species.
plos-pone-0012886:
Li, Preuss, Rilling and co-authors compared the wiring of hand control in chimpanzee brains with their handedness. Most humans are right-handed and show matching left-right differences in the motor pathway from cortex to spine. Chimpanzees also favour one hand at the group level.

Their 2010 study used diffusion MRI, which traces fibre pathways, to measure both sides of this system in chimps. Matching brain asymmetry to hand preference tests how deep the roots of human handedness go. The comparison informs the evolution of brain sidedness itself.  Both chimps and their test scores came from research colonies.
plos-pone-0337786:
Yuri Russo and colleagues set healthy young adults walking a winding raised-stepping course while their eyes and steps were tracked, then added a mental task on top. Adaptive walking normally depends on looking ahead to plan each footfall. Twenty-three volunteers in their late teens and early twenties walked the L-shaped path alone and while thinking hard.

Dual-task walking slowed everyone down, lengthened the time both feet spent grounded, and scattered their gaze toward irrelevant spots with fewer, shorter looks at the stepping targets. Oddly, a sideways cross-step pattern appeared more often without the mental load. Even in the young and fit, the authors show, thinking steals the visual planning that safe walking needs.
plos-pone-0341786:
Paul Leavy, Blánaid Daly, John Ford, and Sara Burke published this 2026 interview study of dentists in Ireland. Private dentists can sign contracts to treat low-income adults under a state scheme, yet many hold back. Nineteen interviews with dentists, officials, and experts were used to build explanations of what drives that choice.

Low payment rates, an outdated menu of covered treatments, and heavy paperwork all discouraged participation, atop weak political backing for oral health. Leavy argues reformers can use these levers to draw dentists back in and widen care for poorer patients.
plos-pone-0342286:
Ye Liang, Louis Shuo Wang, Jiguang Yu, and Xin Zan stress-tested the standard formula doctors use to plan how many patients a new risk prediction model needs. They found it dangerously cheerful when the model aims to be very accurate. Their 2026 Monte Carlo study simulated model development across many settings. It measured the sample size actually required for the model's risk estimates to stay calibrated on fresh patients.

At moderate accuracy targets the formula held up. As targets rose, the true requirement pulled far ahead. At the highest target, the formula's recommended sample routinely produced extreme, unstable risk predictions. That is a separation problem, where the model becomes certain and wrong. The authors advise pairing formula planning with simulation checks whenever a high-accuracy model is promised.
plos-pone-0343186:
Shunsuke Yawata and colleagues asked whether intensive care units that order more blood gas tests in the first day see different death rates. Blood gas tests guide care for unstable patients, yet extra testing carries cost and harm. A Japanese registry covering nearly one hundred and eighteen thousand patients in eighty seven units from 2015 to 2023 was used, with test counts adjusted for patient mix.

Units varied widely in early test use. After adjustment, higher use showed no clear link with hospital death, though a gentle bend hinted at better outcomes at higher use without reaching certainty. More testing alone, the authors conclude, is neither waste nor cure; patient need should drive the count.
plos-pone-0346386:
