Neal Haddaway, Matthew Page, and colleagues introduced PRISMA2020 in 2022, a free software package and web app for drawing the flow diagrams that systematic reviews require. Reporting standards such as PRISMA ask reviewers to account for every study they found, screened, and included. The flow diagram shows that accounting at a glance, letting readers grasp a review's core steps quickly.

The package, built in the R language with an interactive web version, produces diagrams that meet the 2020 standard and can be clicked through for detail. The authors argue this interactivity improves transparency for readers of digital reviews. It is a small tool with an outsized role, since nearly every published systematic review carries one of these diagrams.
poems-pg1186: Poems by Alice Meynell, the refined English poet and essayist of the late Victorian era. Her lyrics on nature, childhood, and faith are crafted with exquisite care, musical and meditative. Less famous than she deserves, Meynell is a poet's poet, treasured by those who find her.
puysegur-suite-memoires-1786:
The Marquis de Puységur published this sequel to his Mémoires in 1786. Two years earlier he had reported artificial somnambulism, the calm trance his patients entered under magnetism. The Suite carries that work further, with new cases and new claims about what the trance reveals.

Puységur's patients, asleep yet speaking, describe their own illnesses and needs. He treats their words as a window into hidden powers of the mind. The focus moves steadily away from Mesmer's fluid toward the inner life. Mesmerism here grows toward psychology in the successor's own words. The sequel marks a turning point that later students of hypnosis still study.
renouvier-esquisse-vol2-1886:
Volume two of Charles Renouvier's systematic classification of philosophical doctrines came out in French in 1886. The first volume, from 1885, laid out his scheme for sorting every school of thought. Renouvier led the French neocritical school. His project grew from a wish to see the whole field at once.

The closing volume carries the survey through the rest of its ground. Doctrines stand ranked by the deep choices they make on freedom, the world, and the soul. Readers can trace how each system grows from a few first commitments. No period English translation exists, so the French text stands alone. Together the volumes form his map.
rimbaud-illuminations-french-1886:
Arthur Rimbaud wrote the poems gathered as Illuminations while still in his teens, then gave up poetry young. The prose poems were first printed in the journal La Vogue in 1886, after he had left literature behind. The text here is the French original of that edition.

In short, blazing pieces Rimbaud paints cities, seas, dawns, and strange pageants. Ordinary scenes tilt suddenly into vision, and the language leaps without warning. He called the pieces colored plates, like prints lit up for the eye. Illuminations helped remake modern poetry, and its free, startling method still shapes poets today. Few books so short have cast so long a shadow.
rosenkreuzer-semler-1786:
German scholar Johann Salomo Semler published an impartial history of the Rosicrucians in 1786. The Rosicrucians were a rumored secret brotherhood of mystics. Tales about them had spread across Europe for over a century.

Semler sifts fact from myth with a scholar's cool eye. He traces the manifestos, the fame, and the claims made for the order. His Enlightenment method treats wonders as claims to test, not truths. The book is dated and dense, yet key. It shows how reason first tackled a legend that still draws seekers today. Few books mark that shift as clearly.
russell-studies-scriptures-vol1-1886:
Charles Taze Russell was a Pittsburgh clothier who founded the Bible Student movement, from which the Jehovah's Witnesses later grew. His Divine Plan of the Ages, published in 1886, is volume one of Studies in the Scriptures. A famous chart inside maps the ages of the world.

Russell reads the Bible as a single plan running from creation through the fall, the gospel age, and the coming millennial kingdom. His chart of the ages, shaped like a pyramid of dispensations, made the scheme visible at a glance. Bible Students studied the volume as their prophetic map of past and future.
sbe-25-manu-1886:
Georg Buhler gave the Laws of Manu English dress in 1886. The work is Book Twenty-Five of the Sacred Books of the East. The Laws of Manu, the Manava Dharma-shastra, is the great law book of the Hindu faith. It claims Manu, the first man, as its source.

Rules deal with birth, caste, food, wed life, and the king's role. The four grades of men and the four stages of life frame the whole scheme. Manu's rules shaped law and custom in India for a vast span of years. Buhler's dress, with its rich notes, is still a stock text.
scheele-chemical-essays-1786:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele reports his trials in The Chemical Essays, in English from 1786. The Swedish apothecary found oxygen before Priestley, and chlorine, acids, and elements followed from his small shop laboratory. He worked alone, tasted and breathed his own discoveries, and died young, experimenting fearlessly to the very end of his short life.

Each essay records a puzzle attacked with simple tools and genius. Airs, earths, and salts yield their secrets one by one here. His modesty hid results that made other men's fame abroad. The volume preserves the heroic age of chemistry in the first person, the lab notes of a quiet master of his art.
secreta-secretorum-1486: Secreta secretorum, 1486. The secret of secrets. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
sidgwick-history-ethics-1886:
Henry Sidgwick published Outlines of the History of Ethics in 1886, a short survey of moral thought. The book was written first for an encyclopedia and then expanded. Sidgwick moves from Greek ethics through Christian teaching to the schools of modern Europe. Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, Hobbes, Kant, and Mill each receive a clear account.

His judgments are calm, fair, and free of party spirit. For generations the Outlines served as the standard short history of ethics in English. Students used it as a map before deeper study. It remains one of the best brief surveys of its kind. Sidgwick's clarity makes hard history easy to follow.
sienkiewicz-deluge-1886:
Henryk Sienkiewicz published The Deluge in 1886, second volume of his Trilogy, the national epic of survival. The Swedish invasion of Poland and Andrzej Kmicic's path from traitor to hero drive its crowded tale. When the book appeared in serial, all Poland read it, and its close was greeted.

Kmicic, a wild young noble, serves the traitor Radziwiłł and is branded a turncoat by the woman he loves. Disguised as Babinicz, he redeems himself in partisan war, at Częstochowa's defense, and in a shot that saves the king. The siege of the Jasna Góra monastery, held against Swedish guns, turns the war and the nation's heart. Oleńka, his beloved, reads his pardon aloud in church in the famous closing scene of public restoration and grace. The Deluge is the Trilogy's heart, Poland's favorite novel of patriotism and redemption.
spurgeon-all-of-grace-1886:
Charles Haddon Spurgeon, the London Baptist preacher whose sermons drew thousands weekly, wrote All of Grace in 1886 for seekers and new converts. The small book is his beloved evangelistic statement of salvation by grace alone. Spurgeon called himself the Prince of Preachers, a title others gave him first.

He walks the reader from God's love for sinners through faith, repentance, and the new birth in short, warm chapters. His aim is not to win arguments but to bring anxious readers to rest in Christ. The book has never gone out of print and still serves as many churches' first gift to inquirers.
stanton-history-woman-suffrage-vol-3-188:
Volume 3 of History of Woman Suffrage appeared in 1886, edited by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage. It covers 1876 to 1885, a decade of steady organizing after the movement's early battles. The documentary method of the first volumes continues here.

State-by-state reports show suffrage campaigns, petition drives, and partial wins such as school-board voting. The volume also records the movement's links with temperance and other reforms of the day. Speeches and letters from dozens of workers, many little known, fill the pages. Together the three volumes form the leaders' own archive of the cause, and Volume 3 carries that archive into the movement's mature years.
stevenson-jekyll-hyde-1886:
Robert Louis Stevenson published The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, a Gothic novella set in London. Dr. Jekyll is a respected doctor with a dark secret. His friend Utterson, a lawyer, worries about Jekyll's link to the brutal Mr. Hyde. Hyde holds a key to Jekyll's house and is named in his will.

A murder and a broken door lead toward a shocking truth. Jekyll has found a way to let his evil side live as a separate man. The tale studies the divided self with great economy. Its names became shorthand for good and evil in one person. Few short books have cast so long a shadow.
stevenson-kidnapped-1886:
Robert Louis Stevenson published Kidnapped in 1886, a novel set in Scotland after the Jacobite rising of 1745. David Balfour, a young orphan, visits an uncle who cheats him and has him shipped to sea. The ship wrecks, and David joins Alan Breck, a bold Jacobite swordsman. Together they witness the Appin murder.

David and Alan flee across the Highlands, hunted as suspects. Their friendship is tested by pride, politics, and danger. Stevenson mixes history with fast adventure and vivid scenery. The chase across moors and glens never slackens. Kidnapped is a high mark in the adventure novel and a love letter to Scotland.
strong-systematic-theology-1886:
Augustus Hopkins Strong was president of Rochester Theological Seminary and the leading Baptist theologian of his day in America. His Systematic Theology, first published in 1886, packs his whole system into a single large volume. Baptist pastors kept it on the shelf beside Hodge.

Strong's system is marked by ethical monism, his view that God's moral nature grounds both law and gospel. He joins Baptist teaching on baptism and the church to wide reading in philosophy and science. The book served as the standard Baptist dogmatics in America for decades after its release. Strong revised the book across his life as his thought grew.
tales-from-shakespeare-pg1286: The Lambs' classic retellings of twenty Shakespeare plays in simple, beautiful prose, prepared for young readers in 1807. Kings, lovers, and villains live again in stories that keep the plots clear and the poetry's spirit alive. This edition offers the book that introduced countless children to Shakespeare.
the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco: Volume five of Lincoln's writings, 1858-1862: from the debates to the war's conduct. The president's mind on the great crisis. History in his own words. The war president's papers are history's backbone, history in his own words.

Volume six of Lincoln's writings, 1862-1863: the Emancipation Proclamation era. The war president at his most momentous. History's turning point in his words. Emancipation and Gettysburg fill these momentous pages, lincoln at his greatest, Lincoln at his greatest.

The last volume of Lincoln’s writings, 1863 to 1865: the war’s end, the second inaugural, and the final letters. “With malice toward none” in its full context. The martyred president’s voice, America’s scripture.
the-secret-of-the-night-pg1686: Gaston Leroux's 1908 thriller sends his young detective Rouletabille into the heart of revolutionary Russia, where nihilist bombs threaten the Tsar's court. Secret passages, narrow escapes, and political murder pile up in the author's breathless style. The Phantom of the Opera's creator at full adventure throttle.
tob-10086:
Evelyn Underhill gathered shorter writings in The Essentials of Mysticism and Other Essays, covering ground her larger books treated at length. Several pieces explain what mysticism is and how it differs from mere emotion. Others answer critics and clarify points readers had misunderstood.

Taken together, the essays form a compact introduction to her thought: mysticism as a serious way of knowing and loving, open in principle beyond a cloister. Because each essay stands alone, readers can enter at any point. The volume also preserves Underhill arguing in public, in short form, for why the contemplative life matters to ordinary people.
tob-10486:
John Edward Mercer gathered testimony in Nature Mysticism from poets, saints, and ordinary walkers who found something divine outdoors. Mountains, seas, woods, and starlight recur in their accounts. Mercer asks what nature mysticism is, and whether it points beyond nature itself to God.

Part anthology and part argument, the book lets witnesses speak in their own words before Mercer draws conclusions. Some experiences are fleeting moments of unity; others shaped whole lives of prayer. Readers interested in spirituality outside church walls will find a careful early survey, one that treats the natural world as a possible doorway rather than merely scenery for human life.
tob-10786:
H. Stanley Redgrove surveyed alchemy from Egyptian workshops to Paracelsus and the modern laboratory in Alchemy: Ancient and Modern. His guiding question is one of debt: what does modern chemistry owe the art it disowned? Redgrove writes as a sympathizer, but a clear-eyed one.

Experiment is separated from fraud and fantasy as he follows adepts, theories of matter, and the slow professionalizing of chemistry. He defends alchemists against easy ridicule while admitting their central quest failed. For readers curious how gold-making turned toward science, Redgrove offers a balanced introduction that neither worships nor mocks its difficult subject.
tob-4086:
The Green Helmet and Other Poems, from 1910, centers on Yeats's verse play The Green Helmet, which retells Cuchulain's beheading game as a contest of heroic courtesy. Around the play stand poems of love, aging, and disillusion with public life. Yeats's middle manner shows clearly: leaner, tougher, more public than the dreamy early books.

Mythology here is staged as moral trial, with heroes tested on generosity and pride rather than strength alone. Personal lyrics admit gray hair and cooling passion with dry honesty. Readers tracing Yeats's development will find the volume a hinge, closing the Celtic twilight period and opening the road toward the stark greatness of his later collections.
tob-4286:
Volume two of Budge's Gods of the Egyptians completes the 1904 survey with studies in Egyptian mythology proper. Myths of creation, the wars of Horus and Set, and the books of the underworld receive long treatment. Budge follows the first volume's pantheon into story, ritual, and tomb text.

The Duat, Egypt's land of the dead, gets its full geography of gates, judges, and fields. Rituals by which priests served the gods daily stand beside the tales told about them. Verified from the 1919 edition, the second half rounds out Budge's most ambitious popular work. Egypt's religion stands here as one vast, strange system.
tucker-state-socialism-anarchism-1886:
Benjamin Tucker published State Socialism and Anarchism in 1886, the manifesto of American individualist anarchism. Tucker edited the journal Liberty in Boston and was the chief voice of his school. The essay began as an address and became the text his readers handed to newcomers.

Tucker sets two systems side by side: state socialism, which would cure monopoly with a bigger state, and anarchism, which would cure it with liberty. The state itself, he argues, is the chief invader, the source of the monopolies that grind the poor. His cure is the free market without privilege, no ruler and no favorites. The essay states the creed of the Boston anarchists with Yankee bluntness. It remains the shortest full account of a distinct American radical tradition, proud, logical, and stubbornly individual.
un-ga-res-a-69-86:
More than six decades of aid to Palestine refugees stand behind Resolution A/69/86, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the 1948 vote on Palestine and the 1949 vote that set up the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, known as UNRWA. For over sixty years, the refugees have borne the loss of their homes, lands, and means of life.

The Assembly affirms that a just fix to the refugee question is a must for lasting peace in the region. UNRWA's role is called vital. Its schools, clinics, relief, and camp works, down to small loans and shelter in crises, have eased the refugees' plight since its first days.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/86 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, deals with assistance to Palestine refugees. It deals with the work of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, UNRWA. It notes with regret that the return or compensation promised in resolution 194 (III) has never been carried out. It affirms that the Agency's work must continue across Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and the Occupied Palestinian Territory. It calls on donors to meet its needs. It invites Brazil and the United Arab Emirates onto its Advisory Commission.
un-sc-res-1286: Resolution 1286 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1999. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-1386: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 1386, and the catalog dates it 2001. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1486: With Resolution 1486, the fifteen members of the Security Council recorded a formal decision in 2003. The entry reproduces the official text through its English Wikisource transcription. Preamble paragraphs lay out the situation as the Council saw it; the operative part then says what must happen, who must act, and what gets reported back.
un-sc-res-1586:
UNMEE was extended under a cloud on 14 March 2005. Ethiopia had massed troops near the Temporary Security Zone, causing concern. The Boundary Commission was closing its field offices for want of progress on marking the border. Ethiopia still rejected key parts of the Commission's ruling. The mission had kept the zone's integrity intact, the Secretary-General reported.

The Council extended UNMEE's present mandate until 15 September 2005. Both parties were called to pull back from any rise in troop levels near the zone. They had to work fully and swiftly with the mission in carrying out its tasks. The Council stressed that Ethiopia and Eritrea bore the main duty for keeping the peace between them. Ethiopia was called, without preconditions, to start applying the Boundary Commission's decision and to open the talks needed to mark the line. Eritrea was pressed to lift the limits it placed on the mission's movement.
un-sc-res-1686: Adopted in 2006, Resolution 1686 is a Security Council decision kept in official-record form through Wikisource. The members who passed it acted under the Charter's peace and security powers. Their text, preserved whole in this entry, moves from stated grounds to numbered decisions, the pattern by which the Council turns discussion into obligation.
un-sc-res-1786:
The Yugoslav war crimes tribunal gained a new chief prosecutor in late 2007. On 28 November 2007 the Security Council appointed Serge Brammertz to the post. The Secretary-General had put his name forward. His term would start on 1 January 2008 and run for four years. The Council could end it early when the tribunal's work was done. The tribunal statute sets this method of appointment.

Brammertz took over as the court pressed toward its completion targets. Resolution 1503 had urged it to finish trials by the end of 2008. All work was meant to end in 2010. The Belgian lawyer had earlier led the United Nations probe into a major political assassination in Lebanon.
un-sc-res-186:
Fighting between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots put Cyprus in danger at the start of 1964. The Council judged that the situation could threaten international peace and security. It could also get worse unless more steps were taken quickly. Resolution 186 was adopted unanimously in March 1964. Later records date it to 4 March 1964.

The Council called on all states to do nothing that could worsen the situation. Cyprus's government was told to take every measure to stop the violence and bloodshed. Both communities were urged to show restraint. The Council recommended creating a United Nations peacekeeping force for Cyprus, with the government's consent. The force would serve for three months at first. Its job was to prevent more fighting and to help restore law, order, and a return to normal conditions. A mediator was also to be named, to work for a peaceful settlement.
un-sc-res-1886: Resolution 1886 stands in the Security Council's numbered series, preserved here in official-record wording. The transcription source is English Wikisource. Its structure follows the body's practice across the decades covered by this collection: grounds first, in the preamble's clauses; action second, in the operative paragraphs. The entry keeps the practice on full display.
un-sc-res-286:
A wave of airliner hijackings alarmed the world in September 1970. Gunmen had seized planes and held passengers and crews hostage. On 9 September 1970 the Security Council appealed for their release. Everyone held after a hijacking had to be freed without exception. The Council voiced grave concern at the threat to innocent lives. Interference with international travel itself drew its rebuke.

States had to take all possible legal steps against hijacking. The aim was to prevent further seizures and protect civil air travel. The resolution came during the Dawson's Field crisis in Jordan. Several airliners were blown up days later. The text is an early building block of aviation security law.
un-sc-res-386:
Mozambique cut all trade and communication links with Southern Rhodesia, and the Security Council backed the move on 17 March 1976. Its president had announced the move on 3 March. Rhodesia's illegal minority regime answered with provocative and aggressive acts, including armed incursions. The Council praised Mozambique for applying the sanctions set by resolution 253 (1968) in full.

The Council condemned Rhodesia's attacks and noted Mozambique's urgent special economic needs, which flowed from the cost of closing its border. It appealed to all states to give Mozambique urgent help with money and goods. United Nations bodies were asked to organize an assistance effort at once, led by the Secretary-General. The text rests on Articles 49 and 50 of the Charter, which cover aid to states harmed by carrying out United Nations measures.
un-sc-res-786:
Bosnia's skies are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 786, adopted on 10 November 1992. A month earlier, the Council had banned military flights over Bosnia and Herzegovina. Reports already suggested that some planes were breaking the ban. Monitors on the ground could not yet prove the breaches.

The text restates the flight ban for all fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft. It backs a plan to place United Nations and European observers at airfields in the region. The United Nations Protection Force grows so it can run the checks. All flight requests must now go through that force, with aid flights given a clear path.
un-sc-res-86: Indonesia won the Security Council's blessing for a UN seat in Resolution 86, passed on 26 September 1950. The Council finds that the Republic of Indonesia is a peace-loving state. It meets the tests laid down in Article 4 of the Charter for those who would join the UN. The Council thus urges the General Assembly to admit the Republic to membership. The vote was ten to none, with China holding back. Freedom from Dutch rule had come the year before.
un-sc-res-986:
Iraq's people were short of food and medicine when the Security Council created the oil-for-food scheme on 14 April 1995. Sanctions from resolution 661 (1990) barred Iraqi oil sales. The Council voiced concern at the grave state of nutrition and health in Iraq and at the risk of worse to come. It called the scheme a temporary measure until Iraq met the Council's demands.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council let states permit imports of Iraqi oil worth up to one billion dollars every ninety days. Each purchase needed approval from the sanctions committee, and payment went in full into an escrow account run by the Secretary-General. A share was also authorized for Turkey, tied to the pipeline route. The funds could pay only for humanitarian needs and other listed purposes, with fair distribution to all parts of Iraq. Independent accountants would inspect the account.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1286, adopted on 19 January 2000, concerns the conflict in Burundi and the Arusha peace process. The Council warmly endorses the choice made by the Eighth Arusha Regional Summit on 1 December 1999. The choice was Nelson Mandela, the former president of South Africa, as the process's new Facilitator. It welcomes the meeting he convened in Arusha on 16 January 2000 to launch his effort.

The Council condemns the continuing violence by all parties, including attacks on civilians. It strongly condemns the murder of UNICEF and World Food Programme staff and Burundian civilians in Rutana province in October 1999. It calls on parties still outside the process to stop fighting and join it. It demands safe humanitarian access, including to the regroupment camps. It asks neighbouring states to halt cross-border insurgent activity and the illicit flow of arms.

Kabul gets an international security force in this text of 20 December 2001. The Bonn Agreement had asked the Council to consider sending such a force, and Afghan leaders welcomed the idea. Security in the capital was the first need of the new Interim Authority.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the International Security Assistance Force for six months. Its job was to help the Interim Authority keep security in Kabul and nearby areas, so Afghan officials and United Nations staff could work safely. States taking part could use all necessary measures to carry out the task, and the Council called on states to contribute troops, equipment, and other support.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended to 15 December 2003 in this text of 11 June 2003. The island's government agreed the force was still needed. A partial easing of limits on movement across the island had raised the force's workload and drawn goodwill from both communities.

The mandate is renewed, and adding up to 34 civilian police officers to the force is backed to meet that workload. Limited steps by the Turkish Cypriot side to ease restrictions placed on UNFICYP in 2000 are noted, while more are pressed for. As before, urgent work on the fate of missing persons is called for, with a report due by 1 December 2003.

Resolution 1586, adopted unanimously on 14 March 2005, extends the UN mission between Ethiopia and Eritrea while the border dispute hardens. UNMEE had kept the temporary security zone intact, the Secretary-General reported. But Ethiopian troops were concentrating in worrying numbers near the zone, and the boundary commission, starved of cooperation, was closing its field offices for lack of progress on marking the line.

UNMEE's mandate was renewed for six months, to September 2005. The Council restated its full support for the Algiers peace agreements and the commission's 2002 ruling, accepted by both parties as final and binding. Its frustration shows through: a peace treaty existed, a border ruling existed, and only demarcation, the last step, was being blocked.

The investigation into the Beirut bombing is extended until 15 June 2007 on 15 June 2006. The commission, created the year before, helps Lebanon investigate the February 2005 attack and other attacks in the country since October 2004. Its latest report found real progress but said the investigation was not yet complete.

The commission's professional work under hard conditions is praised, and Lebanon's request for more time is noted. Its powers to gather evidence and question witnesses in Lebanon stay in place. The commission is to keep reporting on progress, and those behind the attacks, the text restates, must be held accountable for their crimes.

A Belgian jurist took the Yugoslavia court's top trial job by this vote of 2007. On 28 November, the Council adopted Resolution 1786. Serge Brammertz had led the UN probe into the killing of Lebanon's former prime minister. The Secretary-General now put him forward for The Hague. The court's sitting prosecutor was stepping down at year's end.

The text appoints Brammertz as prosecutor, starting on the first day of 2008. His term runs four years. The term can end early once the court's work is done. The finish plan's dates are recalled in the text. Trials were to close by the end of 2008, all work by 2010. Brammertz took over the hunt for the last fugitives. The top Bosnian Serb wartime leaders were seized in 2008 and 2011.

In early 1964, the Security Council created a peace force for Cyprus. It adopted Resolution 186 without dissent. Violence between Greek and Turkish Cypriots had pushed the island toward wider war. The Council warned that the crisis threatened world peace. It also quoted the Charter ban on force against a state's land or freedom.

The text calls on all member states to shun any act that could worsen the crisis. It asks the Cyprus government to take extra steps to restore law and order. Above all, it sets up the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP). The mission was meant to last months. It became one of the longest-running peacekeeping efforts in UN history.

Sierra Leone's integrated peacebuilding office, UNIPSIL, is extended for one year on 15 September 2009, until 30 September 2010. The office had succeeded the earlier integrated office in 2008 and won praise for its peacebuilding work. Sierra Leone's Agenda for Change set the government's development priorities through 2012.

UNIPSIL's mandate stays in place, and the Secretary-General is asked to develop benchmarks to measure its progress and guide an eventual exit. The government, the office, and all partners are called on to align their help with the Agenda for Change. Reports are due every six months. The focus stays on jobs for young people, anti-corruption work, and building state capacity after the civil war.

Air travel faced a new kind of terror in September 1970. Gunmen seized plane after plane that month. Hostages sat on desert strips while the world watched. Crews and travelers were held as bargaining chips. Resolution 286 passed on 9 September 1970, in the heart of that wave.

The Council spoke to all sides at once. Every hostage and crew member had to be freed at once, with no one left out. States were then told to act in law. They had to take all steps they could to stop fresh seizures. They had to guard civil air travel from such acts. The short text was the UN's first word on a crime that would haunt the skies for decades.

Mozambique paid a high price for its stand on Rhodesia. Resolution 386, passed by all members on 17 March 1976, is the Council's reply. That month Mozambique had cut all trade and road and rail links with Rhodesia. It did so to obey the Council's bans on the white-led rebel state. Rhodesia hit back with raids.

The Council praised the choice to cut the links. It condemned Rhodesia's armed attacks on Mozambique. It asked all states to send aid at once: cash, skills, and goods. It asked UN aid bodies, the World Bank, and the Fund to help as well. The aim was to keep the bans strong without wrecking Mozambique's own growth.

Bosnia's no-fly zone is tightened by Resolution 786, adopted in November 1992. Resolution 781 had banned military flights over Bosnia and Herzegovina, but possible violations were reported, and UNPROFOR lacked the technical means to confirm them. The ban was meant to keep aid flights safe and help end the fighting. Monitors from UNPROFOR and the European Community were already deploying at airfields in the region.

The Council reaffirms the ban on all military flights, fixed-wing and rotary, apart from the exceptions in Resolution 781. It endorses the Secretary-General's concept of operations for watching the ban and approves a larger UNPROFOR strength to carry it out. All flight authorization requests must now go to UNPROFOR, with special provision for UN and humanitarian flights. The Council warns it will urgently consider further steps to enforce the ban if new violations are reported.

Indonesia had fought its way to independence from the Netherlands, and in 1950 it asked to join the United Nations. Resolution 86 was adopted on 26 September 1950. The Council found that the Republic of Indonesia is a peace-loving state. It also found that Indonesia met the conditions for membership laid down in Article 4 of the Charter. On that basis, the Council recommended to the General Assembly that Indonesia be admitted to membership in the United Nations.

Resolution 986, adopted unanimously on 14 April 1995, creates the oil-for-food program for Iraq. Sanctions imposed after the invasion of Kuwait had left Iraqi civilians facing a serious nutrition and health emergency. The Council wanted a temporary channel for relief that did not lift the pressure on Baghdad to meet its disarmament obligations.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council let states allow imports of Iraqi oil worth up to one billion dollars every ninety days. Each sale needed approval from the sanctions committee, and the money was earmarked for humanitarian purchases spread fairly among all parts of the Iraqi population. The arrangement grew into the largest aid program the UN had run, and later into a major corruption scandal.
un-un-res-third-report-of-the-secretary-:
Early 2000 in Sierra Leone is the subject of the third report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Mission there, document S/2000/186. UNAMSIL was expanding under the Lomé peace deal, taking over ground once watched by a far smaller team. Rebel compliance with the deal was already in doubt.

The report reviews troop arrivals, disarmament camps, and friction with rebel commanders. It flags the illegal diamond trade as a driver of the war. It asks the Council for patience and support. Months later the mission faced its worst crisis, which this report quietly foreshadows.
waite-mysteries-of-magic-1886:
Young A. E. Waite brought a French sage to English fans in The Mysteries of Magic, his digest of 1886. The sage was Eliphas Levi, the chief voice of the occult in France. No full English text of Levi yet stood on shelves. Waite chose, cut, and turned the best of him into English prose.

His picks stress creed and sign more than rite. Fans in London got their first true taste of Levi here. The book lit a path that Waite's full texts later paved. It marks the start of his long reign in the field. Levi's own books were dear and hard to get in London then. Waite's cheap digest put his thought in reach of clerks and keen youth.
was-ist-die-alchemie-oder-etwas-zu-lache: Was ist die Alchemie? 1786. What is alchemy? This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
weishaupt-apologie-der-illuminaten-1786:
Adam Weishaupt, founder of the Illuminati, published his Apologie der Illuminaten at Frankfurt and Leipzig in 1786. Bavaria had banned his order and seized its papers. The Apologie is his own defense of the order's aims and methods, written while the suppression pressed on him and his followers.

Weishaupt argues that the order sought to make men wiser and freer through education. He answers the charges of plotting against throne and altar. The book is the indispensable counterpart to the hostile seized-papers publications. One side of the story shouts from the state's volumes; here the founder answers at last. Any judgment of the Illuminati must weigh his defense beside the archive.
zola-his-masterpiece-1886:
Vizetelly edited His Masterpiece, Zola's novel of 1886 about art and failure. Chapter one finds the painter Claude out at two in the morning by the town hall. A July storm bursts as he wanders the central markets, in love with Paris at night.

Rain drives him across the Pont Louis Philippe toward his studio on the Isle of St. Louis. Lightning bares the old houses, their balconies, terraces, and carved garlands. Claude Lantier will chase one perfect canvas for the rest of his life. The chase destroys him in the end. Zola drew on his Impressionist friends, and Cezanne never forgave the portrait.
